The following morning, the cells were stimulated with T Cell Activation/Expansion Kit, human
(Supplementary Data 14) at a ratio of 1 bead per 5 cells, along with IL-23 (50 ng/mL) and IL-1β
(50 ng/mL), with or without the addition of PGE2 (1 μM) for 6 hours.

Bulk ATAC and RNA sequencing
ATAC-seq libraries were prepared from 50,000 cells from each of the two stimulation conditions
per study participant according to published protocols with minor modifications107,108. To avoid
difficulties in estimating molarity for optimal cluster density during sequencing, size selection of
ATAC-seq libraries was performed using Pippin Prep with a 2% agarose gel cassette (Sage
Sciences), targeting fragments between 140 and 650 bp. Library quantification was assessed
using Bioanalyzer High Sensitivity DNA chip (Agilent Technologies) and KAPA Library
Quantification qPCR assays. Both ATAC-seq libraries from 33 study participants passed quality
control and were subsequently sequenced. HiSeq PE Rapid Cluster Kit v2 (PE–402–4002, Illumina)
and HiSeq Rapid SBS Kit v2 (200 Cycle) (FC–402–4021, Illumina) were used for sequencing of
library pools performed on HiSeq 2500 sequencers (Illumina) in Rapid Run Mode with 50 bp
paired-end sequencing (15 pairs of libraries). Later sequencing was performed on NextSeq 500
sequencers (Illumina) using High Output v2 (150 cycles) kits (15058247, Illumina), generating 75
bp paired-end sequencing, which was adopted for cost-effectiveness upon availability.

Following ATAC-seq library preparation, remaining cells from each treatment condition were
stored in QIAzol (QIAGEN) at -80°C for subsequent batch-extraction of total RNA. The quality and
concentration of extracted RNA were assessed using a Bioanalyzer and Quant-iT RiboGreen RNA
Assay Kit (Q33140, Invitrogen). For RNA-seq library preparation, the TruSeq Stranded Total RNA
Library Prep Gold (48 Samples) (20020598, Illumina) was used according to the manufacturer’s
protocol. Library pools containing up to 4 paired RNA-seq samples underwent 75 bp paired end
sequencing on NextSeq 500 sequencers using High Output v2 kits, resulting in a total of 38 pairs
of RNA samples being sequenced.

All sequencing was performed on distinct samples.

Raw DOGMA-seq sequencing data processing
The sequenced RNA and ATAC libraries were processed and aligned to GRCh38 human reference
genome using Cell Ranger ARC software (version 2.0.1). This software provided UMI counts, peak
counts, and fragments for each barcode. Joint cell calling was conducted to distinguish cells from
the background based on RNA UMIs per barcode and ATAC transposition events in peaks per
barcode, resulting in the generation of filtered UMI count and peak count matrices. The
sequenced ADT and HTO libraries were aligned using the kallisto | bustools workflow (kallisto
version 0.46.1, bustools version 0.39.3)109, resulting in the generation of raw UMI count matrices,
which were subsequently filtered according to the barcodes in the filtered UMI count and peak
count matrices for RNA and ATAC libraries. Cell demultiplexing was carried out based on the
filtered UMI count matrices for the HTO libraries using the function HTODemux() from the R
package Seurat (version 4.1.0)110, and only singlets remained for downstream analyses.

Peak calling, quality control, and integration of DOGMA-seq data
To obtain a consistent set of ATAC peaks for cells sequenced in different libraries, peaking calling
was performed for all singlets using the function CallPeaks() from the R package Signac (version
1.5.0)111, which invokes MACS2 (version 2.2.7.1)112 to call peaks based on fragments from all
libraries. Subsequently, counts in each called peak were quantified for all singlets using the
FeatureMatrix() function from Signac. A new peak count matrix based on the consistent set of
ATAC peaks across all libraries was generated to enable comparative analysis of chromatin
accessibility across libraries and mitigates batch effects between different libraries.

Filtered UMI count matrices for all RNA and ADT libraries were separately merged, resulting in
two UMI count matrices for RNA and ADT data containing only singlets. To ensure high-quality
data, quality control was conducted based on the three matrices containing only singlets.
Specifically, singlets were filtered with the following criteria applied: a minimum of 200 genes
detected, a minimum of 1,000 total RNA UMIs observed, a maximum of 20% mtRNA reads, a
maximum of 50 ADT UMIs from nine isotype controls observed, a minimum of 1,000 ATAC
fragments observed, and a minimum TSS enrichment score of 4. The remaining high-quality
singlets were subjected to downstream analyses.

For RNA data, regularized negative binomial regression (SCTransform)113 was used to normalize
the UMI count matrix, with glmGamPoi114 invoked to improve the speed and the variable
percent.mt regressed out. 3,000 highly variable genes were identified and used in principal
component analysis (PCA) dimensionality reduction. To mitigate batch effects, Harmony115 was
run on the first 50 components of PCA reduction, with distinct study participants serving as the
covariate and the maximum number of rounds set as 20. Stimulation conditions were not used
as a covariate to run Harmony due to our paired study design. Samples from the same study
participant but treated under different conditions were sequenced in the same batch, and
therefore, any observed variation between samples from the same study participant was
expected to be primarily due to biological differences rather than batch effects. The first 30
Harmony-adjusted components were used in Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection
(UMAP)116 dimensionality reduction.

For ADT data, centered log ratio (CLR) transformation was used to normalize the UMI count
matrix. All 163 protein tags were set as variable features and used in PCA dimensionality
reduction. To mitigate batch effects, Harmony was run on the first 50 components of PCA
reduction, with distinct study participants and whether cryopreserved serving as the covariates
and the maximum number of rounds set as 20. Significant batch effects were observed at the
ADT level between fresh frozen and cryopreserved cells but not at the RNA or ATAC levels.
Therefore, whether or not cryopreserved served as an additional covariate to be adjusted only in
ADT data. The first 30 Harmony-adjusted components were used in UMAP dimensionality
reduction.

For ATAC data, Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI)117 was used to normalize and reduce the
dimensionality of the peak count matrix, with all the peaks selected as variable features. To
mitigate batch effects, Harmony was run on the first 50 components of LSI reduction, with
distinct study participants serving as the covariate and the maximum number of rounds set as 20.
The first 30 (excluding the first component due to correlation with sequencing depth) Harmony-
adjusted components were used in UMAP dimensionality reduction.

The Seurat function FindMultiModalNeighbors() was executed using the Harmony-adjusted
components from all three modalities as described above, followed by UMAP dimensionality
reduction based on the constructed weighted nearest neighbor (WNN) graph. In addition, a
similar process was performed, but only using components from the ADT and ATAC data.
Preliminary clustering was conducted using the SLM algorithm with a resolution of 0.2, based on
the WNN graphs or shared nearest neighbor (SNN) graphs for each modality.

Preliminary cell-type annotation was carried out using a reference-mapping approach. Anchors
at the RNA level were identified between DOGMA-seq data and Azimuth PBMC reference110.
Subsequently, cell type labels were transferred from the reference to DOGMA-seq data, and
clusters mainly consisting of non-T cells were filtered out, ensuring that only T cells were included
in the subsequent analyses. As a result of these quality control and filtering steps, 171,829 high-
quality T cells remained.

Peak calling was repeated for the remaining T cells, resulting in a peak count matrix containing
235,469 ATAC peaks. Additionally, the RNA UMI count matrix contained 36,601 genes, while the
ADT UMI count matrix contained 163 protein tags. The normalization, dimensionality reduction,
batch correction, and preliminary clustering steps described above were also repeated at each
modality for the remaining T cells. chromVAR (version 1.16.0)118 was run using the JASPAR2020
motif set to calculate the enrichment of chromatin accessibility at different TF motif sequences
in each cell.

Definition of activated and resting scores
To address the dynamic changes in T cells upon activation, we computed activated/resting scores
for each cell based on two lists of signature genes, which were derived from bulk RNA-seq data
profiling CD4+ T cells cultured with and without anti-CD3/CD28 beads. Cano-Gamez et al. isolated
naïve (CD25-CD45RA+CD45RO-) and memory (CD25-CD45RA-CD45RO+) CD4+ T cells from PBMCs,
cultured them separately with (activated) or without (resting) anti-CD3/anti-CD28 coated beads
for 16 hours or five days61. Bulk RNA-seq was performed on the cultured cells
(EGAD00001005291), and four lists of differentially expressed (DE) genes were identified for each
cell type and time point, comparing the activated and resting states.

Signature genes for the activated state were defined as DE genes with log2-fold change (LFC) > 1
and FDR-adjusted P-value (FDR) < 0.05, while signature genes for the resting state were defined
as those with LFC < -1 and FDR < 0.05. To ensure stringency, only the overlapping signature genes
between naïve and memory T cells across two time points were defined as the final lists of
signature genes for activated (containing 925 genes) and resting states (containing 1,761 genes),
which were used to calculate activated and resting scores based on RNA data using the Seurat
function AddModuleScore().

Cell type annotation of DOGMA-seq data
To overcome the computational challenge raised by the large DOGMA-seq dataset, cell type
annotation was conducted using a two-stage approach. First, a representative subset of 20,000
T cells was randomly down-sampled from the original 171,829 high-quality T cells. The
normalization, dimensionality reduction, and batch correction steps described above were
repeated at each modality for the representative subset. Clustering was conducted using the SLM
algorithm with a resolution ranging from 0.02 to 0.2, based on the WNN graphs or SNN graphs
for each modality. The R package clustree119 was used to determine the minimum resolution
needed to identify biologically meaningful clusters.

Based on the WNN graph combining ADT and ATAC data, five biologically meaningful clusters can
be easily identified. To identify subclusters within each cluster, iterative normalization,
dimensionality reduction, batch correction, and clustering steps were executed. Canonical
markers at RNA, ADT, and ATAC levels (listed in Supplementary Fig. 2A, C, D) were examined in
each subcluster, as well as the activated/resting scores. The subclusters within the five clusters
were subsequently annotated as distinct subtypes of T cells.

After identifying the 20 subtypes of T cells in the representative subset, the reference-mapping
approach was used to transfer cell type labels to the original 171,829 high-quality T cells. Label
transfer was conducted individually for each library (171,829 cells split by libraries), with
predicted labels merged at the end. Anchors were identified at RNA, ADT, and ATAC levels using
the annotated subset as a reference, resulting in three matrices of prediction scores for each cell
type based on the three modalities. To integrate the prediction scores across the three modalities,
a consensus strategy was utilized, where cells were assigned the labels with the highest
prediction scores across the three modalities.

To support future annotation efforts of Th1 and Th17 cells, we have developed epigenetic and
transcriptomic marker panels specific to these subsets, comparing them to all other CD4+
memory T cells (Supplementary Data 16-19).

Integrative analysis of in-house and public DOGMA-seq data
Mimitou et al. cultured PBMCs in complete medium with (STIM) or without (CTRL) anti-CD3/anti-
CD28 beads for 16 hours54, and the cells were subjected to DOGMA-seq (GSE156478). Following
the same procedure as above, 21,057 T cells were identified for integrative analysis. Counts in
the same set of 235,469 ATAC peaks were quantified for all cells based on the assumption that
the set of ATAC peaks in public DOGMA-seq data is expected to be a subset of the 235,469 ATAC
peaks.

A subset of 20,000 T cells was randomly down-sampled from the annotated in-house DOGMA-
seq data, remaining the previously calculated activated/resting scores. Raw RNA and ATAC data
from in-house and public DOGMA-seq data were integrated, with batch effects between the two
sources corrected by Harmony. Notably, ADT data were not used in the integration process, as
distinct panels of protein tags were added in the two experiments. The UMAP plots shown in
Supplementary Fig. 4 were based on ATAC data since those based on both RNA and ATAC data
or RNA data only were less distinct.

Analysis of DOGMA-seq data under different stimulation conditions
To compare the effects of the four distinct stimulation conditions, 84,345 cells from the first
DOGMA-seq experiment (7 study participants x 4 conditions) were extracted. The same
normalization, dimensionality reduction, and batch correction (using only distinct study
participants as the covariate) steps as described above were repeated at each modality, followed
by UMAP dimensionality reduction using components of both ADT and ATAC data. Next, the
activated/resting scores were recalculated for the extracted cells. Two-sided paired Wilcoxon
tests were also performed to compare the changes in cell type proportions upon different
stimulations. P

To focus on the effects of PGE2, 129,845 cells stimulated under conditions with and without PGE2
were extracted from the 25 study participants (25 study participants x 2 conditions), which were
subjected to a similar analysis as described above.

Cell type-specific differential accessibility (DA) and differential expression (DE) analysis
To compare the changes in chromatin accessibility, gene expression, and protein abundance
upon PGE2 stimulation (Act_IL1B_IL23_PGE2 vs. Act_IL1B_IL23), DA and DE analyses were
performed in each cell type using the pseudo-bulk method, which was expected to outperform
generic and specialized single-cell DE methods120. The R package Libra (version 1.0.0) was
modified to allow for paired samples when employing DESeq2 (version 1.34.0)’s likelihood ratio
test (LRT). Specifically, for each cell type, pseudo-bulk samples were generated by summing peak
counts and gene counts of all cells from the specific cell type and one of the 50 samples (25 study
participants x 2 conditions). The resulting P-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the
FDR method, and the significance level was defined as FDR-adjusted P-values < 0.05. For DA
analysis, ATAC peaks were annotated based on their top linked genes, or in cases where no linked
genes were identified, the nearest genes were used for annotation.

To summarize significant DE genes identified in each cell type, Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA)121
was performed based on all available canonical pathways curated by IPA. For each cell type,
genes with FDR-adjusted P-values < 0.05 were used as inputs. Since the bulk data analysis
identified more than 8,000 genes with FDR-adjusted P-values < 0.05, we used an FDR-adjusted P-
value threshold of < 10-7 to select genes as inputs, in order to comply with IPA’s limitation of a
maximum of 8,000 genes.

To compare the results obtained from DOGMA-seq data with those from bulk data enriched for
Th17 and Treg cells, pseudo-bulk samples were generated by summing peak counts and gene
counts of all cells from the comparable cell types (activated and resting Th17 and CD4+ regulatory
T cells) and one of the 50 samples. The resulting pseudo-bulk samples merging four cell types
were subjected to a similar analysis as described above.

Raw bulk sequencing data processing
The sequenced ATAC libraries were trimmed and aligned to GRCh38 human reference genome
using Bowtie2 (version 2.4.5)122 in very sensitive mode. Reads with MAPQ scores less than 20,
aligned to chrM, and located in genomic blacklist regions annotated by ENCODE were filtered out,
as well as duplicated reads. Counts in the same set of 252,371 ATAC peaks as DOGMA-seq data
were quantified for all samples based on the assumption that the set of ATAC peaks in bulk data
is expected to be a subset of the 252,371 ATAC peaks.

The sequenced RNA libraries were trimmed, aligned to GRCh38 human reference genome using
STAR (version 2.7.6a)123, and quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.1)124 through the nf-core
(version 2.7.2)125 RNA-seq pipeline (version 3.4). The resulting matrices of gene and transcript
counted for 29,972 genes and 87,725 transcripts.

Analysis of bulk ATAC and RNA data
DA analysis was performed on ATAC data using DESeq2’s likelihood ratio test (LRT) in 66 samples
(33 study participants x 2 conditions) to compare the effects of PGE2 stimulation while allowing
for paired samples. Similarly, DE analysis was performed on RNA data using DESeq2’s likelihood
ratio test (LRT) in 76 samples (38 study participants x 2 conditions) to assess the effects of PGE2
stimulation while allowing for paired samples. The resulting P-values were adjusted for multiple
testing using the FDR method, and the significance level was defined as FDR-adjusted P-values <
0.05.

The correlations between effects obtained from bulk analysis and comparable single-cell analysis
were examined, and signals with consistent directions and FDR-adjusted P-values < 0.05 in both
bulk and sing-cell analyses were defined as replicated signals.

Peak-to-gene linkages were also identified in bulk data based on the 64 samples (32 study
participants x 2 conditions) subjected to both ATAC-seq and RNA-seq. Specifically, both ATAC and
RNA data were VST-normalized, and correlations between peaks and genes within a distance of
1M bps were assessed using the R package MatrixEQTL (version 2.3) with a linear model and no
covariates.

Germline variant calling from single-cell multimodal omics data
We used Monopogen126 to accurately detect individual genotypes at each genomic site using
single-cell DOGMA-seq data. Separate BAM files were generated for ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data
for each sample, enabling independent SNP calling from the two modalities. Genotype data
derived from ATAC-seq and RNA-seq were subsequently merged, and discordant calls between
the two datasets were excluded to maintain consistency. To ensure data integrity, duplicate
variants and flipped alleles were removed. Additionally, genotypes with sequencing depth below
a threshold of 10 reads were filtered to improve reliability.

To facilitate integration across samples, we consolidated genotype data from all individuals,
enabling SNP calling directly from the combined dataset to capture variants shared among the
samples. To further enhance the quality of the final genotype dataset, we applied a missingness
filter with a threshold of 0.5, retaining genotypes with sufficient data coverage across the
samples. Identified SNPs were then compared against the SNPs from 1000 Genomes Project
(1KGP)127 to identify shared variants.

After resolving discordances, the two datasets were merged. Duplicate variants and flipped
alleles were removed, and SNPs with missingness greater than 0.5 were filtered out, resulting in
a final set of 60,962 SNPs across 25 samples. Among the identified SNPs, the majority (68.0%)
were called from chromatin accessibility data, 13.9% were derived from gene expression data,
and 18.1% were called from both data modalities. A substantial overlap was observed between
the identified SNPs and those cataloged in the 1KGP127 , with overlap proportions of
approximately 93.3% for chromatin accessibility-derived SNPs and 95.6% for gene expression-
derived SNPs.

Allele-specific gene expression and chromatin accessibility
For the called genotype data, phasing of all biallelic common variants was performed using
shapeit4 (version 4.1.3)128 to distinguish SNPs mapping to maternal versus paternal alleles.
Selection of heterozygous sites was carried out using SelectVariants from GATK (version 4.5.0.0),
and allelic gene expression and peak reads at each heterozygous site were counted using GATK
ASEReadCounter129,130. To detect maximal allelic imbalance, the allelic peak reads for each
heterozygous SNP in each sample were summed. Only biallelic SNP sites with a total of at least
10 reads and a minimum of 2 reads for each allele were retained131,132. Finally, a binomial test
was employed to ascertain significant differential accessibility between alleles, considering the
alternate read counts as success trials and total read counts as trials. The threshold of FDR-
adjusted p < 0.05 was considered as significant.

To evaluate the concentration of IBD-related signals within ASoC/ASE SNPs, we compared these
with the P-value distributions from IBD GWAS summary statistics6. A quantile-quantile (QQ) plot
was then generated to visually evaluate the P-value distribution, aiding in the detection of
potential deviations from the expected uniform distribution. This was achieved by calculating the
expected and observed -log10 transformed P-values for each group, allowing us to visually
inspect for signals of true association as opposed to mere noise. To quantify the differences
between the observed and expected P-value distributions, we employed the Wilcoxon log-rank
sum test.

Enrichment of GWAS SNPs in ATAC peaks
The analysis assessed two sets of fine-mapped GWAS SNPs: the first combines 4,329 SNPs for IBD
from 151 credible sets identified in two studies6,70, and the second includes 4,950 SNPs for 21
autoimmune diseases51. IBD SNPs were further divided into six groups based on their specificity
to CD and UC, as well as whether they are lead variants in credible sets of SNPs. Genome
coordinates of two sets of GWAS SNPs were converted from GRCh37 to GRCh38 for consistency.
Variants in strong linkage disequilibrium (LD) with R2> 0.8 were then identified for each of the 27
lists of SNPs (21 autoimmune diseases + 6 groups of IBD SNPs) using CHEERS (master branch)71,
based on the European-ancestry GRCh38 LD files provided by CHEERS.

The peak count matrix containing 252,371 ATAC peaks was used to generate 500 pseudo-bulk
samples (20 cell types x 25 study participants) by summing peak counts of all cells from a specific
cell type and study participant. The resulting pseudo-bulk samples were then normalized using
CHEERS. For each list of SNPs, CHEERS computed the enrichment of SNPs in the 252,371 ATAC
peaks across the 500 pseudo-bulk samples, resulting in enrichment P-values per sample. Next,
the most conservative methods were used to combine enrichment P-values at the cell type level.
Specifically, individual P-values for each cell type were combined using Fisher’s method, resulting
in 20 combined P-values, which were further adjusted using Bonferroni’s method across the 20
cell types.

When considering stimulation conditions, a similar analysis was performed but confined to cells
under conditions with and without PGE2. In this analysis, 12 study participants were randomly
selected from the 25 study participants, and 480 pseudo-bulk samples (20 cell types x 2
conditions x 12 study participants) were generated by summing peak counts of all cells from a
specific cell type and one of the 12 selected study participants. Down-sampling was necessary
due to computational challenges, as the running time of CHEERS on 500 pseudo-bulk samples
had already reached the 6-day wall time of the computational cluster. To compare the
differences in enrichment between conditions with and without PGE2, individual P-values were
converted to Z-scores, which were compared between conditions using two-sided paired t-tests.

Heritability enrichment analysis
Heritability enrichment analysis through the Stratified Linkage Disequilibrium Score Regression
(S-LDSC) method allows for a nuanced understanding of how genetic variants contribute to
disease heritability133,134. S-LDSC operates by partitioning heritability across different genomic
annotations, enabling researchers to assess whether certain genetic markers or regions are more
significantly associated with a trait than would be expected by chance. This method relies on the
principle that genetic variants in linkage disequilibrium (LD) with causal variants will collectively
contribute to the trait's heritability. By correlating the degree of LD (measured as LD score) with
trait heritability, S-LDSC can estimate the per-SNP heritability attributable to specific genomic
features.

To further validate the enrichment of specific T cell subtypes in IBD GWAS, we applied the S-LDSC
method to partition heritability for IBD, CD and UC6,70 with 53 baseline annotations alongside
binary annotations specific to each T cell subtype75,76. In our analysis, we employed Wilcoxon
rank sum test within Seurat110 to identify the differentially accessible chromatin regions for each
cell type within the samples without PGE2 simulation. From this, we selected the top 20% of DA
peaks by P value for each cell type, extending the region of interest by adding 100-kb windows
to both sides of these peaks. SNPs located within these expanded regions were annotated as '1',
whereas all other SNPs received a '0' annotation. The 503 European individuals from the 1KGP
were included as our LD reference panel127,135. We set a rigorous Bonferroni correction threshold
at the P-value of 8.33 x 10-4, accounting for adjustments across 3 traits and 20 cell types.

Cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages
To reduce the substantial noise in the correlative analysis of sparse single-cell data, the ArchR
(version 1.0.1) function addPeak2GeneLinks() was used to generate low-overlapping aggregates
of cells for each cell type, which were used to identify peak-to-gene linkages within a distance of
1M bps with FDR-adjusted P-values < 0.05. On average, the analysis identified 1,556,942 peak-
to-gene linkages (ranging from 391,031 to 3,393,196) for the 20 cell types.

To obtain more conservative results, cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages were replicated in
pseudo-bulk analysis. Specifically, for each cell type, pseudo-bulk samples were generated by
summing peak counts and gene counts of all cells from the specific cell type and one of the 64
samples (7 study participants x 4 conditions + 18 study participants x 2 conditions). For each cell
type, pseudo-bulk ATAC and RNA data were normalized across the 64 samples using variance
stabilizing transformation (VST) from DESeq2136. Then, correlations between peaks and genes
within a distance of 1M bps were assessed using the R package MatrixEQTL137 with a linear model
and no covariates.

Cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages identified using ArchR were retained as plausible linkages
for downstream analysis if they were replicated in pseudo-bulk analysis with consistent direction
and raw P-value < 0.05. On average, 101,972 plausible peak-to-gene linkages (ranging from
42,724 to 197,245) were retained for the 20 cell types, which correspond to approximately 6.5%
of peak-to-gene linkages initially discovered using ArchR.

The nearest genes for ATAC peaks were annotated using HOMER (version 4.11)138 based on the
hg38 (GRCh38) human reference genome. The top linked genes with the highest significance
were then assessed to determine whether they were also the nearest genes for specific peaks.

SCARlink analysis
To further investigate the effects of cis-regulatory elements and validate the results of our
previous ArchR peak-to-gene linking analysis using single-cell multi-omics data, we applied a
single-gene level model, SCARlink81, to identify potential cell type-specific enhancers of genes.
This method begins by dividing chromatin accessibility data into 500 bp tiles. For each gene,
regions spanning 250 kb upstream to 250 kb downstream of the gene body were selected to
extract tile-level chromatin accessibility features from scATAC-seq data.

SCARlink employs regularized Poisson regression to predict single-cell gene expression based on
single-cell chromatin accessibility. From the regression coefficients, cell type-specific Shapley
values are calculated for each tile to determine their relative importance. Tiles with high Shapley
values are often associated with enhancers, suggesting the presence of potential regulatory
elements within or near those regions. This approach thus enables the identification of putative
cell type-specific enhancers for individual genes.

For this analysis, we randomly selected 50,000 cells from our DOGMA-seq dataset and focused
on 5,000 HVGs. Genes with sparse expression (defined as having more than 90% zero values) were
excluded. For each retained gene, SCARlink models were trained, and Shapley values for
tiles within each gene region were computed and subsequently standardized using z-score
transformation. The significance of the difference in gene expression prediction with and without
a specific tile was assessed on held-out test cells using a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with
FDR adjustment applied to account for multiple hypothesis testing. These computations were
performed across all 20 T cell subtypes to systematically evaluate the enhancer potential of
specific tiles.

Colocalization of GWAS SNPs and plausible peak-to-gene linkages
CHEERS provides a general assessment of the enrichment pattern of GWAS SNPs, narrowing
down the cell types worth exploring, but it may lack the granularity for each locus. A
complimentary analysis was performed to map the two sets of fine-mapped GWAS SNPs
described above to the 252,371 ATAC peaks, especially those linked with nearby genes. The set
of SNPs associated with autoimmune diseases was mapped to 668 ATAC peaks, for which a total
of 7,587 plausible cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages were identified across the 20 cell types.
Similarly, the set of SNPs associated with IBD was mapped to 460 ATAC peaks, for which a total
of 4,877 plausible cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages were identified across the 20 cell types.

To explore a specific disease of interest, the corresponding list of SNPs was mapped to peaks
linked with nearby genes, with a focus on the cell types prioritized by CHEERS. Specifically,
plausible cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages in the prioritized cell types were extracted if the
peaks of these linkages were mapped by the disease-associated SNPs. The results were then
summarized in a gene-centric manner by counting the number of SNPs within linked peaks for a
specific gene across all prioritized cell types. The locus around the gene with the highest number
of SNPs mapping to its linked peaks across all prioritized cell types was selected for visualization.
Cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages mapped by SNPs around the locus were also visualized
at the pseudo-bulk level. We also evaluated the overlap between SCARlink gene-linked tiles,
colocalized IBD SNPs, and plausible peak-to-gene linkages to explore their potential regulation
via enhancer elements.

Cell type-specific colocalization of IBD SNPs, DA peaks, peak-to-gene linkages, and DE genes
To investigate the potential relevance of ATAC peaks mapped by IBD SNPs upon PGE2 stimulation,
colocalization analysis was performed to establish a connection between IBD SNPs, DA peaks,
peak-to-gene linkages, and DE genes for each cell type.

The analysis began by identifying all linked genes for each DA peak in each cell type and examining
whether any of these linked genes were also DE genes. By doing so, linked DE genes for each DA
peak were identified through peak-to-gene linkages, and the consistency among the three types
of signals was checked. For example, if both a DA peak and its linked DE genes were up-regulated
upon PGE2 stimulation, a positive peak-to-gene linkage was expected for a consistent signal. DA
peaks consistently linked with at least one DE gene were hypothesized to be crucial upon PGE2
stimulation through the regulation of the linked DE genes. Next, the overlap between ATAC peaks
mapped by IBD SNPs and DA peaks consistently linked with at least one DE gene was extracted
and defined as the colocalization of IBD SNPs, DA peaks, peak-to-gene linkages, and DE genes.

The same colocalization analysis was also performed in bulk data and used as a replication for
some of the results identified in the single-cell analysis of the 20 cell types. Selected colocalization
signals were subsequently visualized using scatter plots to depict peak-to-gene linkages and
boxplots to depict DE genes and DA peaks, as well as a highlight for IBD SNPs falling within the
DA peaks.

Following the colocalization analysis, 72 out of the 151 IBD credible sets, encompassing 633 IBD-
associated SNPs participating in colocalization events, were prioritized, implicating a total of 325
genes. Subsequently, a Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis139,140 was performed on these
325 genes to identify overrepresented pathways.
