## Methods

Enrichment and stimulation of peripheral blood T Cells
25 healthy young adult human study participants (ages 18-35 years) were enrolled with informed
consent in a research protocol compliant with all relevant ethical regulations, which was
approved by the University of Pittsburgh Institutional Review Board. T cells were enriched from
15 ml of whole blood following the MACSxpress Whole Blood Pan T Cell Isolation Kit, human
(Supplementary Data 14) protocol. T cells from the first seven study participants were cultured
immediately following isolation, while those from the remaining 18 study participants were
cryopreserved in CryoStor CS10 (BioLife Solutions) at a concentration of up to 10 million cells per
ml for subsequent processing.

For T cells from the first seven study participants (the first series of DOGMA-seq experiments),
four aliquots of one million cells each per study participant were cultured in 24-well cell culture
plates (Falcon) and stimulated overnight for 12 hours in 1 ml X-VIVO 15 Serum-free
Hematopoietic Cell Medium (Lonza) with 10 ul ImmunoCult Human CD3/CD28/CD2 T Cell
Activator (Supplementary Data 14), 50 ng/ml IL-1B (R&D Systems), and 50 ng/ml IL-23 (R&D
Systems), with either 1 uM Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) (Sigma) or 3 ng/ml TGF-beta1 (R&D Systems),
or both, for a total of four stimulation conditions per participant. After the overnight incubation,
cells were collected into 15 ml conical tubes through a 30-um strainer and washed with up to 14
ml of PBS/0.2% BSA, centrifuged at 300 g for 10 minutes at 4°C, and resuspended in 50 ul
Pharmingen Stain Buffer (BSA) (BD Bioscience). An aliquot of each cell suspension was then
stained with ViaStain AOPI Staining Solution (Nexcelom Bioscience) and viability counts were
obtained using a Cellometer Auto 2000 Cell Viability Counter (Nexcelom Bioscience).

For T cells from the remaining 18 study participants (the second series of DOGMA-seq
experiments), cells from four participants at a time were thawed and two aliquots of one million
cells each per study participant were cultured in 24-well cell culture plates and stimulated
overnight for 12 hours in 1 ml X-VIVO 15 Serum-free Hematopoietic Cell Medium with 10 ul
ImmunoCult Human CD3/CD28/CD2 T Cell Activator, 50 ng/ml IL-1B, and 50 ng/ml IL-23, with or
without 1 uM PGE2, for a total of two stimulation conditions per participant. After overnight
incubation, cells were collected into 15 ml conical tubes through a 30-um strainer and washed
with up to 14 ml of PBS/0.2% BSA, centrifuged at 300 g for 10 minutes at 4°C, and resuspended
in 50 ul Pharmingen Stain Buffer. An aliquot of each cell suspension was then stained with
ViaStain AOPI Staining Solution and viability counts were obtained using a Cellometer Auto 2000
Cell Viability Counter.

Cell staining with barcoded antibodies
For the first series of DOGMA-seq experiments, after a 10-minute incubation with Human
TruStain FcX (BioLegend) on ice, up to 700,000 cells from each condition were stained with 1.4 ul
of a unique TotalSeq-A anti-human Hashtag antibody (Supplementary Data 14) in 70 ul for 30
minutes at 4°C on a Laminar Wash 16-well strip (Curiox Biosystems), for a total of 8 samples. Cells
were washed in the Laminar Wash Mini System (Curiox Biosystems) with 25 cycles at a flow rate
of 10 ul/s. Following cell collection and counting, up to 1 million cells from the different
hashtagged samples were pooled, centrifuged at 350g for 5 minutes at 4°C and resuspended in
50 ul. Fifty ul of TotalSeq-A Human Universal Cocktail, V1.0 (Supplementary Data 14-15), at a 0.5
dilution, were added to the cells and the total volume was split between 2 wells of a Laminar
Wash 16-well strip for a 30-minute incubation at 4°C. Cells were washed as previously described,
pooled into a 300 ul volume of PBS/0.2% BSA, filtered through a 40 um Scienceware Flowmi Cell
Strainer (SP Bel-Art) and counted.

For the second series of DOGMA-seq experiments, after a 10-minute incubation with Human
TruStain FcX on ice, approximately 300,000 cells from each condition were stained with 1 ul of a
unique TotalSeq-A anti-human Hashtag antibody in 50 ul for 30 minutes at 4°C on a Laminar Wash
16-well strip, for a total of 8 samples. Cells were washed in the Laminar Wash Mini System (Curiox
Biosystems) with 25 cycles at a flow rate of 10 ul/s. Following collection and cell count, up to 1.5
million cells from the different hashtagged samples were pooled, centrifuged at 350g for 5
minutes at 4°C and resuspended in 50 ul. Fifty ul of TotalSeq-A Human Universal Cocktail, V1.0,
at a 0.5 dilution, were added to the cells and the total volume was split between 2 wells of a
Laminar Wash 16-well strip for a 30-minute incubation at 4°C. Cells were washed as previously
described, pooled into a 300 ul volume of PBS/0.2% BSA, filtered through a 40 um Scienceware
Flowmi Cell Strainer and counted.

Single cell preparation for DOGMA-seq
The two series of DOGMA-seq experiments were conducted following the same protocol.
Specifically, cells were processed according to the CG000338 Chromium Next GEM Multiome
ATAC + Gene Expression Rev. D protocol (10X Genomics) for Gene Expression and ATAC library
construction using the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression 4 rxn
kit (1000285, 10X Genomics) while modifications for DOGMA-seq were done following the “Cell
permeabilization with Digitonin (CDIG)” section of the DOGMA-seq protocol (NYGC Innovation
Lab).

Up to 1 million cells were centrifuged at 350g for 5 minutes at 4°C and permeabilized in 100 ul
chilled DIG lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl , 0.0075% Digitonin
2
(Invitrogen) and 2 U/ul Protector RNase inhibitor (Roche Diagnostics)) for 1 min on ice, followed
by the addition of 1 ml of chilled DIG wash buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 3 mM
MgCl and 1 U/ul RNase inhibitor) and pipette mixing, before centrifugation at 500g for 5 minutes
2
at 4°C. The supernatant was discarded, the pellet was resuspended in a very small volume of
about 17 ul of diluted Nuclei Buffer (10X Genomics) and 5 ul were used for cell counting.
Following the CG000338 Chromium Next GEM Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression Rev. D protocol,
30,000 cells were processed for each of two transposition reactions, then added to a Barcoding
master mix and loaded into two wells of a Chip J and run on the Chromium Controller (10X
Genomics) for GEM generation.

During sample pre-amplification (step 4.2), ADT and hashtag oligonucleotide (HTO) additive
primers were added to a final concentration of 0.2 uM. After cleanup and elution in 100 ul, 30 ul
of the eluate were set aside for ADT and 10 ul were set aside for HTO i7 index PCR reactions that
were performed using Illumina TruSeq™ Small RNA RPIX (with custom indexes) and Illumina
TruSeq D70X_short primers, respectively, and the SI-PCR primer.

When generating the Gene Expression library in the Chromium Next GEM Multiome protocol, we
chose to use the Single Index Kit T Set A (1000213, 10X Genomics) instead of the Dual Index Kit
TT Set A (1000215, 10X Genomics).

Initial cDNA concentrations and ATAC library average sizes were determined by the TapeStation
High Sensitivity D5000 assay using HS D5000 Reagents (5067-5593, Agilent Technologies) and HS
D5000 ScreenTape (5067-5592, Agilent Technologies), and Gene Expression, ADT and HTO library
average sizes were determined by the TapeStation High Sensitivity D1000 assay using HS D1000
Reagents (5067-5585, Agilent Technologies) and HS D1000 ScreenTape (5067-5584, Agilent
Technologies) on the 2200 TapeStation System (Agilent Technologies). Library concentrations
were assessed by Qubit dsDNA HS assays (Q32851, Invitrogen). The Qubit concentration together
with the average size of fragments from the TapeStation assay were used to calculate the
estimated molarity of each library. The estimated molarity determined the dilutions necessary to
perform library quantification using the KAPA Library Quantification Kit, Universal (07960140001,
Roche Diagnostics) for each sample in order to obtain a more accurate molarity concentration of
the library pool for sequencing.

DOGMA-seq library pooling for sequencing
For the first series of DOGMA-seq experiments, libraries from DOGMA-seq experiments were
pooled and sequenced with libraries from other projects. The DOGMA-seq RNA libraries were
represented at either 0.81 nM or 2.14 nM, DOGMA-seq ADT libraries were represented at either
0.39 or 1.05 nM and HTO libraries at either 0.05 or 0.13 nM in two separate 10 nM pools of
libraries that were submitted to the UPMC Genome Center and sequenced using a NovaSeq 6000
S4 Reagent Kit v1.5 (200 cycles) (20028313, Illumina) on a NovaSeq 6000 sequencer (Illumina)
with a configuration 28/8/0/T151 (187 total cycles). DOGMA-seq ATAC libraries were represented
at approximately 2.5 nM and 5 nM in two separate 10 nM pools that were sequenced using using a
NovaSeq 6000 S1 Reagent Kit v1.5 (100 cycles) (20028319, Illumina) with a configuration
53/8/24/53 (138 total cycles).

For the second series of DOGMA-seq experiments, libraries from the DOGMA-seq experiments
were pooled and sequenced with libraries from other projects. The DOGMA-seq RNA libraries
were represented at approximately 1 nM, ADT libraries were represented at approximately 0.5
nM and HTO libraries at approximately 0.06 nM in two separate pools of libraries that were
submitted to the UPMC Genome Center and sequenced using a NovaSeq 6000 S4 Reagent Kit
v1.5 (200 cycles) on a NovaSeq 6000 sequencer with a configuration of either 28/10/10/151 (199
total cycles) or 28/8/0/151 (187 total cycles). DOGMA-seq ATAC libraries were represented at
either 1 nM or 2 nM in two separate pools that were sequenced using either a NovaSeq 6000 S4
Reagent Kit v1.5 (200 cycles) on a NovaSeq 6000 sequencer with a configuration of 100/8/24/100
(232 total cycles) or a NovaSeq 6000 S2 Reagent kit v1.5 (100 cycles) (20028316, Illumina) on a
NovaSeq 6000 sequencer with a configuration of 53/8/24/53 (138 total cycles).

All sequencing was performed on distinct samples.

Activation and stimulation of CD4+CD45RO+CD196+ peripheral blood T cells
39 healthy young adult human study participants (ages 18-35 years) were enrolled with informed
consent in a research protocol, which was approved by the University of Pittsburgh Institutional
Review Board. CD4+ T cells were enriched from 50 mL of peripheral blood using the RosetteSep
Human CD4+ T Cell Enrichment Cocktail (Supplementary Data 14) and sorted for
CD4+CD45RO+CD196+ cells using fluorescence-activated cell sorting. The sorted cells were then
incubated overnight at 1×106 cells/mL in serum-free X-VIVO-20 medium (Lonza) at 37°C, 5% CO2.
The following morning, the cells were stimulated with T Cell Activation/Expansion Kit, human
(Supplementary Data 14) at a ratio of 1 bead per 5 cells, along with IL-23 (50 ng/mL) and IL-1β
(50 ng/mL), with or without the addition of PGE2 (1 μM) for 6 hours.

Bulk ATAC and RNA sequencing
ATAC-seq libraries were prepared from 50,000 cells from each of the two stimulation conditions
per study participant according to published protocols with minor modifications107,108. To avoid
difficulties in estimating molarity for optimal cluster density during sequencing, size selection of
ATAC-seq libraries was performed using Pippin Prep with a 2% agarose gel cassette (Sage
Sciences), targeting fragments between 140 and 650 bp. Library quantification was assessed
using Bioanalyzer High Sensitivity DNA chip (Agilent Technologies) and KAPA Library
Quantification qPCR assays. Both ATAC-seq libraries from 33 study participants passed quality
control and were subsequently sequenced. HiSeq PE Rapid Cluster Kit v2 (PE–402–4002, Illumina)
and HiSeq Rapid SBS Kit v2 (200 Cycle) (FC–402–4021, Illumina) were used for sequencing of
library pools performed on HiSeq 2500 sequencers (Illumina) in Rapid Run Mode with 50 bp
paired-end sequencing (15 pairs of libraries). Later sequencing was performed on NextSeq 500
sequencers (Illumina) using High Output v2 (150 cycles) kits (15058247, Illumina), generating 75
bp paired-end sequencing, which was adopted for cost-effectiveness upon availability.

Following ATAC-seq library preparation, remaining cells from each treatment condition were
stored in QIAzol (QIAGEN) at -80°C for subsequent batch-extraction of total RNA. The quality and
concentration of extracted RNA were assessed using a Bioanalyzer and Quant-iT RiboGreen RNA
Assay Kit (Q33140, Invitrogen). For RNA-seq library preparation, the TruSeq Stranded Total RNA
Library Prep Gold (48 Samples) (20020598, Illumina) was used according to the manufacturer’s
protocol. Library pools containing up to 4 paired RNA-seq samples underwent 75 bp paired end
sequencing on NextSeq 500 sequencers using High Output v2 kits, resulting in a total of 38 pairs
of RNA samples being sequenced.

All sequencing was performed on distinct samples.

Raw DOGMA-seq sequencing data processing
The sequenced RNA and ATAC libraries were processed and aligned to GRCh38 human reference
genome using Cell Ranger ARC software (version 2.0.1). This software provided UMI counts, peak
counts, and fragments for each barcode. Joint cell calling was conducted to distinguish cells from
the background based on RNA UMIs per barcode and ATAC transposition events in peaks per
barcode, resulting in the generation of filtered UMI count and peak count matrices. The
sequenced ADT and HTO libraries were aligned using the kallisto | bustools workflow (kallisto
version 0.46.1, bustools version 0.39.3)109, resulting in the generation of raw UMI count matrices,
which were subsequently filtered according to the barcodes in the filtered UMI count and peak
count matrices for RNA and ATAC libraries. Cell demultiplexing was carried out based on the
filtered UMI count matrices for the HTO libraries using the function HTODemux() from the R
package Seurat (version 4.1.0)110, and only singlets remained for downstream analyses.

Peak calling, quality control, and integration of DOGMA-seq data
To obtain a consistent set of ATAC peaks for cells sequenced in different libraries, peaking calling
was performed for all singlets using the function CallPeaks() from the R package Signac (version
1.5.0)111, which invokes MACS2 (version 2.2.7.1)112 to call peaks based on fragments from all
libraries. Subsequently, counts in each called peak were quantified for all singlets using the
FeatureMatrix() function from Signac. A new peak count matrix based on the consistent set of
ATAC peaks across all libraries was generated to enable comparative analysis of chromatin
accessibility across libraries and mitigates batch effects between different libraries.

Filtered UMI count matrices for all RNA and ADT libraries were separately merged, resulting in
two UMI count matrices for RNA and ADT data containing only singlets. To ensure high-quality
data, quality control was conducted based on the three matrices containing only singlets.
Specifically, singlets were filtered with the following criteria applied: a minimum of 200 genes
detected, a minimum of 1,000 total RNA UMIs observed, a maximum of 20% mtRNA reads, a
maximum of 50 ADT UMIs from nine isotype controls observed, a minimum of 1,000 ATAC
fragments observed, and a minimum TSS enrichment score of 4. The remaining high-quality
singlets were subjected to downstream analyses.

For RNA data, regularized negative binomial regression (SCTransform)113 was used to normalize
the UMI count matrix, with glmGamPoi114 invoked to improve the speed and the variable
percent.mt regressed out. 3,000 highly variable genes were identified and used in principal
component analysis (PCA) dimensionality reduction. To mitigate batch effects, Harmony115 was
run on the first 50 components of PCA reduction, with distinct study participants serving as the
covariate and the maximum number of rounds set as 20. Stimulation conditions were not used
as a covariate to run Harmony due to our paired study design. Samples from the same study
participant but treated under different conditions were sequenced in the same batch, and
therefore, any observed variation between samples from the same study participant was
expected to be primarily due to biological differences rather than batch effects. The first 30
Harmony-adjusted components were used in Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection
(UMAP)116 dimensionality reduction.

For ADT data, centered log ratio (CLR) transformation was used to normalize the UMI count
matrix. All 163 protein tags were set as variable features and used in PCA dimensionality
reduction. To mitigate batch effects, Harmony was run on the first 50 components of PCA
reduction, with distinct study participants and whether cryopreserved serving as the covariates
and the maximum number of rounds set as 20. Significant batch effects were observed at the
ADT level between fresh frozen and cryopreserved cells but not at the RNA or ATAC levels.
Therefore, whether or not cryopreserved served as an additional covariate to be adjusted only in
ADT data. The first 30 Harmony-adjusted components were used in UMAP dimensionality
reduction.

For ATAC data, Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI)117 was used to normalize and reduce the
dimensionality of the peak count matrix, with all the peaks selected as variable features. To
mitigate batch effects, Harmony was run on the first 50 components of LSI reduction, with
distinct study participants serving as the covariate and the maximum number of rounds set as 20.
The first 30 (excluding the first component due to correlation with sequencing depth) Harmony-
adjusted components were used in UMAP dimensionality reduction.

The Seurat function FindMultiModalNeighbors() was executed using the Harmony-adjusted
components from all three modalities as described above, followed by UMAP dimensionality
reduction based on the constructed weighted nearest neighbor (WNN) graph. In addition, a
similar process was performed, but only using components from the ADT and ATAC data.
Preliminary clustering was conducted using the SLM algorithm with a resolution of 0.2, based on
the WNN graphs or shared nearest neighbor (SNN) graphs for each modality.

Preliminary cell-type annotation was carried out using a reference-mapping approach. Anchors
at the RNA level were identified between DOGMA-seq data and Azimuth PBMC reference110.
Subsequently, cell type labels were transferred from the reference to DOGMA-seq data, and
clusters mainly consisting of non-T cells were filtered out, ensuring that only T cells were included
in the subsequent analyses. As a result of these quality control and filtering steps, 171,829 high-
quality T cells remained.

Peak calling was repeated for the remaining T cells, resulting in a peak count matrix containing
235,469 ATAC peaks. Additionally, the RNA UMI count matrix contained 36,601 genes, while the
ADT UMI count matrix contained 163 protein tags. The normalization, dimensionality reduction,
batch correction, and preliminary clustering steps described above were also repeated at each
modality for the remaining T cells. chromVAR (version 1.16.0)118 was run using the JASPAR2020
motif set to calculate the enrichment of chromatin accessibility at different TF motif sequences
in each cell.

Definition of activated and resting scores
To address the dynamic changes in T cells upon activation, we computed activated/resting scores
for each cell based on two lists of signature genes, which were derived from bulk RNA-seq data
profiling CD4+ T cells cultured with and without anti-CD3/CD28 beads. Cano-Gamez et al. isolated
naïve (CD25-CD45RA+CD45RO-) and memory (CD25-CD45RA-CD45RO+) CD4+ T cells from PBMCs,
cultured them separately with (activated) or without (resting) anti-CD3/anti-CD28 coated beads
for 16 hours or five days61. Bulk RNA-seq was performed on the cultured cells
(EGAD00001005291), and four lists of differentially expressed (DE) genes were identified for each
cell type and time point, comparing the activated and resting states.

Signature genes for the activated state were defined as DE genes with log2-fold change (LFC) > 1
and FDR-adjusted P-value (FDR) < 0.05, while signature genes for the resting state were defined
as those with LFC < -1 and FDR < 0.05. To ensure stringency, only the overlapping signature genes
between naïve and memory T cells across two time points were defined as the final lists of
signature genes for activated (containing 925 genes) and resting states (containing 1,761 genes),
which were used to calculate activated and resting scores based on RNA data using the Seurat
function AddModuleScore().

Cell type annotation of DOGMA-seq data
To overcome the computational challenge raised by the large DOGMA-seq dataset, cell type
annotation was conducted using a two-stage approach. First, a representative subset of 20,000
T cells was randomly down-sampled from the original 171,829 high-quality T cells. The
normalization, dimensionality reduction, and batch correction steps described above were
repeated at each modality for the representative subset. Clustering was conducted using the SLM
algorithm with a resolution ranging from 0.02 to 0.2, based on the WNN graphs or SNN graphs
for each modality. The R package clustree119 was used to determine the minimum resolution
needed to identify biologically meaningful clusters.

Based on the WNN graph combining ADT and ATAC data, five biologically meaningful clusters can
be easily identified. To identify subclusters within each cluster, iterative normalization,
dimensionality reduction, batch correction, and clustering steps were executed. Canonical
markers at RNA, ADT, and ATAC levels (listed in Supplementary Fig. 2A, C, D) were examined in
each subcluster, as well as the activated/resting scores. The subclusters within the five clusters
were subsequently annotated as distinct subtypes of T cells.

After identifying the 20 subtypes of T cells in the representative subset, the reference-mapping
approach was used to transfer cell type labels to the original 171,829 high-quality T cells. Label
transfer was conducted individually for each library (171,829 cells split by libraries), with
predicted labels merged at the end. Anchors were identified at RNA, ADT, and ATAC levels using
the annotated subset as a reference, resulting in three matrices of prediction scores for each cell
type based on the three modalities. To integrate the prediction scores across the three modalities,
a consensus strategy was utilized, where cells were assigned the labels with the highest
prediction scores across the three modalities.

To support future annotation efforts of Th1 and Th17 cells, we have developed epigenetic and
transcriptomic marker panels specific to these subsets, comparing them to all other CD4+
memory T cells (Supplementary Data 16-19).

Integrative analysis of in-house and public DOGMA-seq data
Mimitou et al. cultured PBMCs in complete medium with (STIM) or without (CTRL) anti-CD3/anti-
CD28 beads for 16 hours54, and the cells were subjected to DOGMA-seq (GSE156478). Following
the same procedure as above, 21,057 T cells were identified for integrative analysis. Counts in
the same set of 235,469 ATAC peaks were quantified for all cells based on the assumption that
the set of ATAC peaks in public DOGMA-seq data is expected to be a subset of the 235,469 ATAC
peaks.

A subset of 20,000 T cells was randomly down-sampled from the annotated in-house DOGMA-
seq data, remaining the previously calculated activated/resting scores. Raw RNA and ATAC data
from in-house and public DOGMA-seq data were integrated, with batch effects between the two
sources corrected by Harmony. Notably, ADT data were not used in the integration process, as
distinct panels of protein tags were added in the two experiments. The UMAP plots shown in
Supplementary Fig. 4 were based on ATAC data since those based on both RNA and ATAC data
or RNA data only were less distinct.

Analysis of DOGMA-seq data under different stimulation conditions
To compare the effects of the four distinct stimulation conditions, 84,345 cells from the first
DOGMA-seq experiment (7 study participants x 4 conditions) were extracted. The same
normalization, dimensionality reduction, and batch correction (using only distinct study
participants as the covariate) steps as described above were repeated at each modality, followed
by UMAP dimensionality reduction using components of both ADT and ATAC data. Next, the
activated/resting scores were recalculated for the extracted cells. Two-sided paired Wilcoxon
tests were also performed to compare the changes in cell type proportions upon different
stimulations. P

To focus on the effects of PGE2, 129,845 cells stimulated under conditions with and without PGE2
were extracted from the 25 study participants (25 study participants x 2 conditions), which were
subjected to a similar analysis as described above.

Cell type-specific differential accessibility (DA) and differential expression (DE) analysis
To compare the changes in chromatin accessibility, gene expression, and protein abundance
upon PGE2 stimulation (Act_IL1B_IL23_PGE2 vs. Act_IL1B_IL23), DA and DE analyses were
performed in each cell type using the pseudo-bulk method, which was expected to outperform
generic and specialized single-cell DE methods120. The R package Libra (version 1.0.0) was
modified to allow for paired samples when employing DESeq2 (version 1.34.0)’s likelihood ratio
test (LRT). Specifically, for each cell type, pseudo-bulk samples were generated by summing peak
counts and gene counts of all cells from the specific cell type and one of the 50 samples (25 study
participants x 2 conditions). The resulting P-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the
FDR method, and the significance level was defined as FDR-adjusted P-values < 0.05. For DA
analysis, ATAC peaks were annotated based on their top linked genes, or in cases where no linked
genes were identified, the nearest genes were used for annotation.

To summarize significant DE genes identified in each cell type, Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA)121
was performed based on all available canonical pathways curated by IPA. For each cell type,
genes with FDR-adjusted P-values < 0.05 were used as inputs. Since the bulk data analysis
identified more than 8,000 genes with FDR-adjusted P-values < 0.05, we used an FDR-adjusted P-
value threshold of < 10-7 to select genes as inputs, in order to comply with IPA’s limitation of a
maximum of 8,000 genes.

To compare the results obtained from DOGMA-seq data with those from bulk data enriched for
Th17 and Treg cells, pseudo-bulk samples were generated by summing peak counts and gene
counts of all cells from the comparable cell types (activated and resting Th17 and CD4+ regulatory
T cells) and one of the 50 samples. The resulting pseudo-bulk samples merging four cell types
were subjected to a similar analysis as described above.

Raw bulk sequencing data processing
The sequenced ATAC libraries were trimmed and aligned to GRCh38 human reference genome
using Bowtie2 (version 2.4.5)122 in very sensitive mode. Reads with MAPQ scores less than 20,
aligned to chrM, and located in genomic blacklist regions annotated by ENCODE were filtered out,
as well as duplicated reads. Counts in the same set of 252,371 ATAC peaks as DOGMA-seq data
were quantified for all samples based on the assumption that the set of ATAC peaks in bulk data
is expected to be a subset of the 252,371 ATAC peaks.

The sequenced RNA libraries were trimmed, aligned to GRCh38 human reference genome using
STAR (version 2.7.6a)123, and quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.1)124 through the nf-core
(version 2.7.2)125 RNA-seq pipeline (version 3.4). The resulting matrices of gene and transcript
counted for 29,972 genes and 87,725 transcripts.

Analysis of bulk ATAC and RNA data
DA analysis was performed on ATAC data using DESeq2’s likelihood ratio test (LRT) in 66 samples
(33 study participants x 2 conditions) to compare the effects of PGE2 stimulation while allowing
for paired samples. Similarly, DE analysis was performed on RNA data using DESeq2’s likelihood
ratio test (LRT) in 76 samples (38 study participants x 2 conditions) to assess the effects of PGE2
stimulation while allowing for paired samples. The resulting P-values were adjusted for multiple
testing using the FDR method, and the significance level was defined as FDR-adjusted P-values <
0.05.

The correlations between effects obtained from bulk analysis and comparable single-cell analysis
were examined, and signals with consistent directions and FDR-adjusted P-values < 0.05 in both
bulk and sing-cell analyses were defined as replicated signals.

Peak-to-gene linkages were also identified in bulk data based on the 64 samples (32 study
participants x 2 conditions) subjected to both ATAC-seq and RNA-seq. Specifically, both ATAC and
RNA data were VST-normalized, and correlations between peaks and genes within a distance of
1M bps were assessed using the R package MatrixEQTL (version 2.3) with a linear model and no
covariates.

Germline variant calling from single-cell multimodal omics data
We used Monopogen126 to accurately detect individual genotypes at each genomic site using
single-cell DOGMA-seq data. Separate BAM files were generated for ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data
for each sample, enabling independent SNP calling from the two modalities. Genotype data
derived from ATAC-seq and RNA-seq were subsequently merged, and discordant calls between
the two datasets were excluded to maintain consistency. To ensure data integrity, duplicate
variants and flipped alleles were removed. Additionally, genotypes with sequencing depth below
a threshold of 10 reads were filtered to improve reliability.

To facilitate integration across samples, we consolidated genotype data from all individuals,
enabling SNP calling directly from the combined dataset to capture variants shared among the
samples. To further enhance the quality of the final genotype dataset, we applied a missingness
filter with a threshold of 0.5, retaining genotypes with sufficient data coverage across the
samples. Identified SNPs were then compared against the SNPs from 1000 Genomes Project
(1KGP)127 to identify shared variants.

After resolving discordances, the two datasets were merged. Duplicate variants and flipped
alleles were removed, and SNPs with missingness greater than 0.5 were filtered out, resulting in
a final set of 60,962 SNPs across 25 samples. Among the identified SNPs, the majority (68.0%)
were called from chromatin accessibility data, 13.9% were derived from gene expression data,
and 18.1% were called from both data modalities. A substantial overlap was observed between
the identified SNPs and those cataloged in the 1KGP127 , with overlap proportions of
approximately 93.3% for chromatin accessibility-derived SNPs and 95.6% for gene expression-
derived SNPs.

Allele-specific gene expression and chromatin accessibility
For the called genotype data, phasing of all biallelic common variants was performed using
shapeit4 (version 4.1.3)128 to distinguish SNPs mapping to maternal versus paternal alleles.
Selection of heterozygous sites was carried out using SelectVariants from GATK (version 4.5.0.0),
and allelic gene expression and peak reads at each heterozygous site were counted using GATK
ASEReadCounter129,130. To detect maximal allelic imbalance, the allelic peak reads for each
heterozygous SNP in each sample were summed. Only biallelic SNP sites with a total of at least
10 reads and a minimum of 2 reads for each allele were retained131,132. Finally, a binomial test
was employed to ascertain significant differential accessibility between alleles, considering the
alternate read counts as success trials and total read counts as trials. The threshold of FDR-
adjusted p < 0.05 was considered as significant.

To evaluate the concentration of IBD-related signals within ASoC/ASE SNPs, we compared these
with the P-value distributions from IBD GWAS summary statistics6. A quantile-quantile (QQ) plot
was then generated to visually evaluate the P-value distribution, aiding in the detection of
potential deviations from the expected uniform distribution. This was achieved by calculating the
expected and observed -log10 transformed P-values for each group, allowing us to visually
inspect for signals of true association as opposed to mere noise. To quantify the differences
between the observed and expected P-value distributions, we employed the Wilcoxon log-rank
sum test.

Enrichment of GWAS SNPs in ATAC peaks
The analysis assessed two sets of fine-mapped GWAS SNPs: the first combines 4,329 SNPs for IBD
from 151 credible sets identified in two studies6,70, and the second includes 4,950 SNPs for 21
autoimmune diseases51. IBD SNPs were further divided into six groups based on their specificity
to CD and UC, as well as whether they are lead variants in credible sets of SNPs. Genome
coordinates of two sets of GWAS SNPs were converted from GRCh37 to GRCh38 for consistency.
Variants in strong linkage disequilibrium (LD) with R2> 0.8 were then identified for each of the 27
lists of SNPs (21 autoimmune diseases + 6 groups of IBD SNPs) using CHEERS (master branch)71,
based on the European-ancestry GRCh38 LD files provided by CHEERS.

The peak count matrix containing 252,371 ATAC peaks was used to generate 500 pseudo-bulk
samples (20 cell types x 25 study participants) by summing peak counts of all cells from a specific
cell type and study participant. The resulting pseudo-bulk samples were then normalized using
CHEERS. For each list of SNPs, CHEERS computed the enrichment of SNPs in the 252,371 ATAC
peaks across the 500 pseudo-bulk samples, resulting in enrichment P-values per sample. Next,
the most conservative methods were used to combine enrichment P-values at the cell type level.
Specifically, individual P-values for each cell type were combined using Fisher’s method, resulting
in 20 combined P-values, which were further adjusted using Bonferroni’s method across the 20
cell types.

When considering stimulation conditions, a similar analysis was performed but confined to cells
under conditions with and without PGE2. In this analysis, 12 study participants were randomly
selected from the 25 study participants, and 480 pseudo-bulk samples (20 cell types x 2
conditions x 12 study participants) were generated by summing peak counts of all cells from a
specific cell type and one of the 12 selected study participants. Down-sampling was necessary
due to computational challenges, as the running time of CHEERS on 500 pseudo-bulk samples
had already reached the 6-day wall time of the computational cluster. To compare the
differences in enrichment between conditions with and without PGE2, individual P-values were
converted to Z-scores, which were compared between conditions using two-sided paired t-tests.

Heritability enrichment analysis
Heritability enrichment analysis through the Stratified Linkage Disequilibrium Score Regression
(S-LDSC) method allows for a nuanced understanding of how genetic variants contribute to
disease heritability133,134. S-LDSC operates by partitioning heritability across different genomic
annotations, enabling researchers to assess whether certain genetic markers or regions are more
significantly associated with a trait than would be expected by chance. This method relies on the
principle that genetic variants in linkage disequilibrium (LD) with causal variants will collectively
contribute to the trait's heritability. By correlating the degree of LD (measured as LD score) with
trait heritability, S-LDSC can estimate the per-SNP heritability attributable to specific genomic
features.

To further validate the enrichment of specific T cell subtypes in IBD GWAS, we applied the S-LDSC
method to partition heritability for IBD, CD and UC6,70 with 53 baseline annotations alongside
binary annotations specific to each T cell subtype75,76. In our analysis, we employed Wilcoxon
rank sum test within Seurat110 to identify the differentially accessible chromatin regions for each
cell type within the samples without PGE2 simulation. From this, we selected the top 20% of DA
peaks by P value for each cell type, extending the region of interest by adding 100-kb windows
to both sides of these peaks. SNPs located within these expanded regions were annotated as '1',
whereas all other SNPs received a '0' annotation. The 503 European individuals from the 1KGP
were included as our LD reference panel127,135. We set a rigorous Bonferroni correction threshold
at the P-value of 8.33 x 10-4, accounting for adjustments across 3 traits and 20 cell types.

Cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages
To reduce the substantial noise in the correlative analysis of sparse single-cell data, the ArchR
(version 1.0.1) function addPeak2GeneLinks() was used to generate low-overlapping aggregates
of cells for each cell type, which were used to identify peak-to-gene linkages within a distance of
1M bps with FDR-adjusted P-values < 0.05. On average, the analysis identified 1,556,942 peak-
to-gene linkages (ranging from 391,031 to 3,393,196) for the 20 cell types.

To obtain more conservative results, cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages were replicated in
pseudo-bulk analysis. Specifically, for each cell type, pseudo-bulk samples were generated by
summing peak counts and gene counts of all cells from the specific cell type and one of the 64
samples (7 study participants x 4 conditions + 18 study participants x 2 conditions). For each cell
type, pseudo-bulk ATAC and RNA data were normalized across the 64 samples using variance
stabilizing transformation (VST) from DESeq2136. Then, correlations between peaks and genes
within a distance of 1M bps were assessed using the R package MatrixEQTL137 with a linear model
and no covariates.

Cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages identified using ArchR were retained as plausible linkages
for downstream analysis if they were replicated in pseudo-bulk analysis with consistent direction
and raw P-value < 0.05. On average, 101,972 plausible peak-to-gene linkages (ranging from
42,724 to 197,245) were retained for the 20 cell types, which correspond to approximately 6.5%
of peak-to-gene linkages initially discovered using ArchR.

The nearest genes for ATAC peaks were annotated using HOMER (version 4.11)138 based on the
hg38 (GRCh38) human reference genome. The top linked genes with the highest significance
were then assessed to determine whether they were also the nearest genes for specific peaks.

SCARlink analysis
To further investigate the effects of cis-regulatory elements and validate the results of our
previous ArchR peak-to-gene linking analysis using single-cell multi-omics data, we applied a
single-gene level model, SCARlink81, to identify potential cell type-specific enhancers of genes.
This method begins by dividing chromatin accessibility data into 500 bp tiles. For each gene,
regions spanning 250 kb upstream to 250 kb downstream of the gene body were selected to
extract tile-level chromatin accessibility features from scATAC-seq data.

SCARlink employs regularized Poisson regression to predict single-cell gene expression based on
single-cell chromatin accessibility. From the regression coefficients, cell type-specific Shapley
values are calculated for each tile to determine their relative importance. Tiles with high Shapley
values are often associated with enhancers, suggesting the presence of potential regulatory
elements within or near those regions. This approach thus enables the identification of putative
cell type-specific enhancers for individual genes.

For this analysis, we randomly selected 50,000 cells from our DOGMA-seq dataset and focused
on 5,000 HVGs. Genes with sparse expression (defined as having more than 90% zero values) were
excluded. For each retained gene, SCARlink models were trained, and Shapley values for
tiles within each gene region were computed and subsequently standardized using z-score
transformation. The significance of the difference in gene expression prediction with and without
a specific tile was assessed on held-out test cells using a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with
FDR adjustment applied to account for multiple hypothesis testing. These computations were
performed across all 20 T cell subtypes to systematically evaluate the enhancer potential of
specific tiles.

Colocalization of GWAS SNPs and plausible peak-to-gene linkages
CHEERS provides a general assessment of the enrichment pattern of GWAS SNPs, narrowing
down the cell types worth exploring, but it may lack the granularity for each locus. A
complimentary analysis was performed to map the two sets of fine-mapped GWAS SNPs
described above to the 252,371 ATAC peaks, especially those linked with nearby genes. The set
of SNPs associated with autoimmune diseases was mapped to 668 ATAC peaks, for which a total
of 7,587 plausible cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages were identified across the 20 cell types.
Similarly, the set of SNPs associated with IBD was mapped to 460 ATAC peaks, for which a total
of 4,877 plausible cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages were identified across the 20 cell types.

To explore a specific disease of interest, the corresponding list of SNPs was mapped to peaks
linked with nearby genes, with a focus on the cell types prioritized by CHEERS. Specifically,
plausible cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages in the prioritized cell types were extracted if the
peaks of these linkages were mapped by the disease-associated SNPs. The results were then
summarized in a gene-centric manner by counting the number of SNPs within linked peaks for a
specific gene across all prioritized cell types. The locus around the gene with the highest number
of SNPs mapping to its linked peaks across all prioritized cell types was selected for visualization.
Cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages mapped by SNPs around the locus were also visualized
at the pseudo-bulk level. We also evaluated the overlap between SCARlink gene-linked tiles,
colocalized IBD SNPs, and plausible peak-to-gene linkages to explore their potential regulation
via enhancer elements.

Cell type-specific colocalization of IBD SNPs, DA peaks, peak-to-gene linkages, and DE genes
To investigate the potential relevance of ATAC peaks mapped by IBD SNPs upon PGE2 stimulation,
colocalization analysis was performed to establish a connection between IBD SNPs, DA peaks,
peak-to-gene linkages, and DE genes for each cell type.

The analysis began by identifying all linked genes for each DA peak in each cell type and examining
whether any of these linked genes were also DE genes. By doing so, linked DE genes for each DA
peak were identified through peak-to-gene linkages, and the consistency among the three types
of signals was checked. For example, if both a DA peak and its linked DE genes were up-regulated
upon PGE2 stimulation, a positive peak-to-gene linkage was expected for a consistent signal. DA
peaks consistently linked with at least one DE gene were hypothesized to be crucial upon PGE2
stimulation through the regulation of the linked DE genes. Next, the overlap between ATAC peaks
mapped by IBD SNPs and DA peaks consistently linked with at least one DE gene was extracted
and defined as the colocalization of IBD SNPs, DA peaks, peak-to-gene linkages, and DE genes.

The same colocalization analysis was also performed in bulk data and used as a replication for
some of the results identified in the single-cell analysis of the 20 cell types. Selected colocalization
signals were subsequently visualized using scatter plots to depict peak-to-gene linkages and
boxplots to depict DE genes and DA peaks, as well as a highlight for IBD SNPs falling within the
DA peaks.

Following the colocalization analysis, 72 out of the 151 IBD credible sets, encompassing 633 IBD-
associated SNPs participating in colocalization events, were prioritized, implicating a total of 325
genes. Subsequently, a Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis139,140 was performed on these
325 genes to identify overrepresented pathways.

### Reviewer 2

The authors conducted an elegant multiomic analysis to explore the connection between inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)
and genetic predisposition, applying a sophisticated computational workflow that, to the best of my knowledge, has not been
previously implemented. Their approach is undoubtedly innovative and contributes valuable insights.
However, the manuscript's structure and flow present challenges, making it difficult for a broad readership to follow. The
extensive use of technical terminology and abbreviations complicates the overall clarity, potentially obscuring the
manuscript's key message.
Despite the novelty of the computational approach and the compelling nature of the study, the work lacks mechanistic
validation of its findings in IBD, which appears to be the primary aim as suggested in the title. Given the complexity of IBD
pathogenesis, attributing T-cell inhibition solely to PGE2 seems overly simplistic. A broader perspective incorporating
additional mechanisms underlying T-cell-mediated immunity in IBD would enhance the work’s depth.
I strongly recommend that the authors refine and streamline the text to improve accessibility while emphasizing the
relevance of their findings to IBD pathogenesis. Expanding the discussion beyond genetic associations to highlight key
inflammatory and immune-mediated pathways—fundamental aspects of IBD—would significantly strengthen the
manuscript's clinical impact.

### Reviewer 3

As a reviewer coming from a clinical/transational background, I am not in a position to fully evaluate the technical aspects of
the DOGMA-seq single-cell multiomics platform. However, I find the characterization and depth of analysis regarding the
number and subsets of T cells quite impressive and commendable.
That said, I believe the claim that this constitutes a model of IBD inflammation—based solely on in vitro stimulation of T cells
with IL-1β, IL-23, and either PGE2, TGF-β, or both—appears overly simplistic. While the approach clearly identifies key
response elements to these specif-ic immune mediators, it does not recapitulate the complex immunopathology of IBD as
seen in patients.
In line with this, I would have appreciated data derived from the DOGMA-seq platform on mucosal T cells obtained from IBD
patients, both during remission and active disease, or from other immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs), to
strengthen translational relevance.
Finally, I would encourage the authors to reflect on whether their DOGMA-seq platform data provide any insights into the
potential relationship between PGE2 signaling and non-response to anti-TNF therapy, an important and clinically relevant
area that may benefit from the mechanistic resolution their platform enables.

more prominently. We now emphasize this finding as a major conclusion of the section,
highlighting its relevance for understanding the genetic architecture of IBD and the stimulation-
dependent regulatory landscape of human T cells.
We hope these changes improve the clarity and impact of this section in line with the reviewer’s helpful
suggestions.
Results: Enrichment of IBD GWAS SNPs in ATAC peaks
The general structure of this section is logical, but it can be improved:
• "Credible SNPs" should be defined briefly when first mentioned.
• CHEERS and S-LDSC are introduced without explaining their purposes in simple terms.
• P-values are listed in dense groups without summarizing the overall patterns or trends.
• Some key biological implications, particularly about activated T cell subtypes mediating IBD
risk, are understated.
• The relevance of PGE2 shifting enrichment patterns is interesting but could be better linked to
clinical observations (e.g., NSAID effects in Crohn's vs UC).
Suggestions:
• Add short, plain-language explanations of credible SNPs, CHEERS, and S-LDSC.
• Summarize biological conclusions first before presenting detailed statistics.
• Conclude the section with a clear statement about the clinical relevance of these findings.
R: We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback. In the revised manuscript, we have made several
changes to improve clarity, interpretation, and clinical relevance in this section:
1. We now define “IBD credible set SNPs” at the point they are first mentioned. We explain that
these SNPs were prioritized based on Bayesian fine-mapping approaches that account for linkage
disequilibrium and effect size, and are comprised of the SNPs in each of 151 fine-mapped IBD
loci which have a greater than 95% probability of containing the causal variant.
2. To aid understanding of the analytical tools used, we have added concise explanations for both
CHEERS and S-LDSC. We describe CHEERS as a method that detects enrichment of disease-
associated SNPs in regulatory regions by accounting for the quantitative, cell-state-specific
activity of chromatin elements. We describe our application of S-LDSC as a heritability-based
method that tests whether GWAS signal is enriched in specific annotations across cell types.
3. We have restructured the paragraph to present biological conclusions first, followed by
supporting statistics. For example, we now summarize that IBD SNPs are most strongly enriched
in activated Th17, Th1, and CD4+ Treg cells, and that CD-associated SNPs show stronger
enrichment in activated states than UC-associated SNPs, before detailing the exact P-values.
4. We have expanded our interpretation of biological trends, emphasizing the prominent role of
activated CD4+ T cell subsets (Th1, Th17, CD4+ Treg) across both CHEERS and S-LDSC results,
which supports their key involvement in IBD pathogenesis.
5. To address the reviewer’s final point, we have revised the last paragraph of the section to
explicitly link PGE2-dependent enrichment pattern shifts to clinical observations that NSAID use,
which is known to reduce endogenous PGE2 levels, is associated with increased relapse risk in
CD but not UC. We state that reduced regulatory flexibility at CD risk loci could increase
vulnerability to PGE2 depletion during NSAID exposure, whereas the comparatively greater
plasticity of UC loci may help buffer against such effects.
We believe these revisions significantly enhance the clarity, biological insight, and translational relevance
of the section and hope they adequately address the reviewer’s concerns.
Results: Cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages
This section is important but could be made easier to follow:
• "Peak-to-gene linkage" should be briefly explained for readers less familiar with single-cell
analysis.
• The use of ArchR is introduced without explaining its role.
• Again, the biological interpretation of the findings should come before listing numbers.
• A short closing statement explaining why this matters (e.g., better annotation of non-coding
disease variants) would strengthen the section.
Suggestions:
• Add short intuitive definitions and interpretations before presenting numbers.
• End the section by framing why these regulatory maps are important for understanding IBD
genetics.
R: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful comments and suggestions regarding the clarity and
interpretability of this important section. In the revised manuscript, we have made several changes to
address these points:
1. We have added a brief, intuitive definition of peak-to-gene linkages early in the section,
explaining that they are correlations between chromatin accessibility peaks and expression levels
of nearby genes, thereby mapping candidate cis-regulatory elements (CREs) to their putative gene
targets.
2. We clarified the role of ArchR as a computational framework for inferring peak-to-gene linkages
from single-cell multi-omic data.
3. To improve readability, we restructured the paragraph so that biological insights appear before
the detailed numerical results. Specifically, we first highlight that peak-to-gene linkages often
reveal regulatory relationships beyond nearest-gene assignments, and that naïve T cells tend to
have fewer such linkages despite their abundance, indicating lower regulatory complexity in their
resting states.
4. Finally, we added a closing sentence emphasizing the significance of these regulatory maps for
IBD genetics. We state that identifying cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages enables more
accurate annotation of non-coding disease variants, and provides mechanistic hypotheses linking
GWAS loci to gene regulation in relevant T cell subsets.
We believe these revisions improve the accessibility and biological interpretation of the section and thank
the reviewer again for helping to strengthen this part of the manuscript.
Results: SCARlink predictions
While SCARlink is a strong addition to the study, it is not well introduced:
• Shapley values are mentioned without explaining what they mean in this context.
• The SCARlink method workflow is not clearly outlined.
• The biological relevance to enhancer prediction for IBD is not made explicit.
• Too many raw numbers are listed before any interpretation.
Suggestions:
• Introduce Shapley values with one sentence explaining the concept intuitively.
• Briefly describe the goal of SCARlink (predicting enhancers linked to gene expression).
• State the biological relevance upfront before listing numbers.
R: We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. In the revised manuscript, we clarify the goal of
SCARlink at the beginning of the section by explicitly stating that it predicts enhancer-gene relationships
using single-cell gene expression and chromatin accessibility data. We also introduce Shapley values as a
measure of the relative importance of fixed-size genomic tiles in explaining the expression of a given gene.
To improve readability, we mention the biological rationale for applying SCARlink, to augment
understanding of cis-regulatory mechanisms and annotation of enhancer elements relevant to IBD in T
cells, earlier in the section. Finally, we have restructured the presentation of the numerical results to
emphasize interpretation first, followed by supporting statistics. These revisions collectively improve the
clarity, accessibility, and biological framing of the SCARlink analysis.
Results: Colocalization of IBD-associated SNPs with CREs and DE genes
This section is better structured, but could still be made more efficient:
• Lists of SNPs and genes (e.g., PTGER4, SATB1, GPR183) are too long and could be grouped
more compactly.
• The biological meaning and clinical relevance of the PTGER4 findings should be more clearly
emphasized.
• Redundancy about PTGER4 could be trimmed slightly.
Suggestions:
• Highlight the major discoveries first (especially PTGER4), and summarize other loci briefly.
• Link the findings more explicitly to mechanisms of IBD pathogenesis.
R: We thank the reviewer for the helpful feedback. In response:
1. We have streamlined the lists of SNPs and genes throughout this section by consolidating
overlapping observations and presenting the PTGER4 locus and associated variants as a single
coherent paragraph. Other loci such as LNPEP, TNFRSF14, IL2RA, CCL20, and CXCR5 are now
described more succinctly in grouped summaries to maintain readability while preserving key
biological insights, such as predicted enhancer activity, peak-to-gene linkages, and supporting
evidence from eQTL and fine-mapping studies.
2. We agree that the biological and clinical relevance of PTGER4 deserved clearer emphasis. We
have revised the text to make our findings more interpretable and mechanistically meaningful.
Specifically, we now highlight that:
2.1 PTGER4 expression is strongly predicted by chromatin accessibility (Spearman R² =
0.244 from SCARlink analysis);
2.2 Multiple IBD SNPs colocalize with enhancer regions linked to PTGER4 across diverse
T cell subsets;
2.3 These findings converge on the PTGER4 locus as a genetically and epigenetically
regulated target in T cells, strongly implicating PGE2–EP4 signaling in IBD pathogenesis;
2.4 The SNP rs10440635 is located in an IBD credible set, was previously implicated in
ankylosing spondylitis, and regulates PTGER4 in synovial biopsies, adding cross-disease
relevance.
3. To address redundancy, we have removed repetitive mentions of colocalization results and
merged previously separated pieces of evidence (e.g. SCARlink predictions) into integrated
summaries for each key region.
4. Finally, we have added a concluding sentence that explicitly links these colocalization results
to mechanistic insights, emphasizing how genetic variants may influence cell type-specific
regulatory programs that contribute to IBD pathogenesis.
Results: Application to Other Immune-Mediated Diseases
The extension to other diseases is an important point but could be framed more cleanly:
• Again, the lists of SNPs and genes are too long and detailed for the main text.
• A short summary of the main diseases and key findings at the start would help.
• The clinical relevance of connecting CD8+ memory T cells to psoriasis, Behçet’s, and SLE could
be emphasized more clearly.
Suggestions:
• Summarize the major disease associations upfront.
• Group minor findings together rather than listing them separately.
• Mention broader translational relevance.
R: We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestions to improve clarity and structure. In the revised
manuscript, we have substantially reorganized this section to highlight the major findings more clearly.
Specifically:
1. We now open the section with a concise summary of the main disease associations, emphasizing
the prominent enrichment of psoriasis-, Behçet’s-, and SLE-associated SNPs in ATAC peaks of
CD8⁺ memory T cells.
2. To enhance readability, we have grouped secondary associations (e.g., those for alopecia areata,
ankylosing spondylitis) into a more compact paragraph, while retaining all corresponding
Supplementary Figures.
3. We have clarified the clinical relevance of the CD8⁺ memory T cell findings by explicitly linking
the genetic enrichment patterns to known effector functions and disease mechanisms in psoriasis,
Behçet’s, and SLE.
4. Finally, we have revised the concluding paragraph to more directly emphasize the broader
translational value of our atlas in illuminating shared regulatory mechanisms and informing future
therapeutic hypotheses across immune-mediated diseases.
Importantly, we preserved all Supplementary Figures to retain the full detail for interested readers, while
improving the narrative focus in the main text as recommended. We hope these revisions address the
reviewer’s concerns.
Discussion
The Discussion undersells the major scientific contributions of this study:
• The opening is too focused on techniques (DOGMA-seq) rather than biological discoveries.
• The important findings regarding PTGER4, Th17/Treg dynamics, and PGE2 in IBD pathogenesis
are not highlighted as they should be.
• There is too much repetition of the Results without synthesis or proposing new models.
• The potential clinical relevance of the findings is understated.
• The final paragraph is too generic; it should more confidently state what new understanding the
study provides.
Suggestions:
• Start with the major biological discoveries, not the techniques.
• Frame a model linking genetic variants, chromatin accessibility, PGE2 signaling, and T cell state
transitions in IBD.
• Highlight translational implications, including PTGER4 as a potential therapeutic target.
• End with a confident, forward-looking conclusion emphasizing the study's impact.
R: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive feedback. In response, we have substantially
revised the Discussion section to better highlight the key biological discoveries and enhance the narrative
synthesis of our findings. Specifically:
1. We have revised the opening paragraph to center the discussion on the biological context and
motivation, rather than beginning with a technical description of DOGMA-seq.
2. We more prominently feature PTGER4 and its dual role as both a dynamically regulated
transcriptional target and a genetically implicated node in the PGE2 signaling pathway. We
emphasize its potential as a translationally actionable therapeutic target in IBD, aligning with the
reviewer’s request to highlight clinical relevance.
3. In the revised Discussion, we propose a model in which PGE2 modulates T cell fate transitions
in an activation-state-dependent manner, intersecting with inherited susceptibility through
chromatin remodeling and gene regulation. We further describe how PGE2 selectively represses
effector programs in activated cells while priming resting cells, offering a novel perspective on
how IBD-relevant microenvironment and genetic factors interact in shaping T cell responses
during disease pathogenesis.
4. To reduce repetition, we have streamlined descriptive results and refocused on conceptual
insights, including the regulatory convergence between responses to PGE2, chromatin
accessibility, and GWAS SNP enrichment in Th17, Th1, and Treg cells.
5. Finally, we have strengthened the concluding paragraph to more confidently articulate the
mechanistic model proposed by this study. Rather than ending with a generic summary, we now
explicitly state how our multi-omic atlas enables identification of disease-relevant regulatory
mechanisms and offers a path forward for precision immunomodulation in IBD and other immune-
mediated disorders.
We believe these revisions significantly improve the clarity and impact of the Discussion. We are grateful
for the reviewer’s insightful suggestions, which helped us better articulate the biological significance and
translational implications of our findings.
Reviewer #2:
Remarks to the Author:
The authors conducted an elegant multiomic analysis to explore the connection between inflammatory
bowel disease (IBD) and genetic predisposition, applying a sophisticated computational workflow that,
to the best of my knowledge, has not been previously implemented. Their approach is undoubtedly innovative
and contributes valuable insights.
However, the manuscript's structure and flow present challenges, making it difficult for a broad readership
to follow. The extensive use of technical terminology and abbreviations complicates the overall clarity,
potentially obscuring the manuscript's key message.
Despite the novelty of the computational approach and the compelling nature of the study, the work lacks
mechanistic validation of its findings in IBD, which appears to be the primary aim as suggested in the title.
Given the complexity of IBD pathogenesis, attributing T-cell inhibition solely to PGE2 seems overly
simplistic. A broader perspective incorporating additional mechanisms underlying T-cell-mediated
immunity in IBD would enhance the work’s depth.
I strongly recommend that the authors refine and streamline the text to improve accessibility while
emphasizing the relevance of their findings to IBD pathogenesis. Expanding the discussion beyond genetic
associations to highlight key inflammatory and immune-mediated pathways—fundamental aspects of
IBD—would significantly strengthen the manuscript's clinical impact.
R: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. In response to these
valuable suggestions, we have made the following revisions to improve the clarity and impact of our
manuscript:
1. We have revised the Introduction and Discussion sections to better highlight the key biological
questions and major discoveries of the study. Specifically, we have restructured the Discussion to
highlight our central findings: the activation state-specific effects of PGE2, its differential
reprogramming of Th17, Th1, and Treg cells, and the mechanistic insights into PTGER4 regulation.
We have also incorporated a conceptual model describing how PGE2 may intersect with genetic
risk variants and regulatory elements to modulate T cell phenotypes relevant to IBD. In doing so,
we have shifted technical descriptions of the DOGMA-seq assay and computational pipelines to
the Methods section, thereby improving accessibility for a broader readership and reducing the
technical density of the main text.
2. To further enhance clarity, we have moved several technical descriptions related to the activation
score to the Methods section. In addition, we have added a table of abbreviations in the
Supplementary Table 18 to assist readers in following the manuscript.
3. In response to the reviewer’s concern about oversimplification of attributing T cell inhibition
solely to PGE2, our study did not aim to fully recapitulate the complex mucosal microenvironment
of IBD. Rather, we used a reductionist approach to study the effects of PGE2, TGF-β, or PGE2
and TGF-β in T cells that were also exposed to activation stimuli, IL-1β, and IL-23 based on
rationales described in the Introduction and the Discussion. We intentionally studied T cells from
healthy, young adult donors to avoid confounding variables such as effects of IBD-directed
medications, comorbidities, and aging on the immune responses that we aimed to study, and to
align with the typical age of IBD onset in adults. Within this well-controlled experimental system,
the observed inhibition and reprogramming effects were indeed primarily attributable to PGE2.
We now more explicitly communicate the motivation for our experimental design and
acknowledge its limitations in the Discussion. Given the current lack of high-resolution single-cell
multi-omic studies specifically investigating the effects of PGE2 in human T cells that are exposed
to activation stimuli, IL-23 and IL-1β, which play key roles in Th17 biology and IBD pathogenesis,
we believe that our dataset lays important groundwork for future patient-based studies.
4. Finally, we have expanded the Discussion to better establish relevance of our findings within
the broader framework of IBD pathogenesis and immune-mediated inflammatory pathways. In
particular, we emphasize how PGE2 signaling interacts with T cell activation states and genetic
architecture, including loci like PTGER4, to modulate transcriptional and epigenetic programs.
We also highlight the translational relevance of these insights, especially the potential of the EP4
receptor for PGE2, encoded by PTGER4, as both a genetically regulated effector and druggable
target. In addition, we point to the broader utility of our single-cell multi-omic T cell atlas as a
resource for exploring shared effector circuits across multiple immune-mediated disorders. While
we acknowledge that functional validation remains an important next step, our study establishes a
mechanistically grounded framework and a set of actionable hypotheses for future investigations,
ranging from CRISPR perturbation studies to patient-derived T cells and in vivo disease models.
We are grateful for the reviewer’s comments, which have helped us improve the clarity, focus, and clinical
relevance of our manuscript. We hope that the revised version more effectively communicates both the
conceptual novelty and the broader translational potential of our findings.
Reviewer #3:
Remarks to the Author:
As a reviewer coming from a clinical/transational background, I am not in a position to fully evaluate the
technical aspects of the DOGMA-seq single-cell multiomics platform. However, I find the
characterization and depth of analysis regarding the number and subsets of T cells quite impressive and
commendable.
That said, I believe the claim that this constitutes a model of IBD inflammation—based solely on in vitro
stimulation of T cells with IL-1β, IL-23, and either PGE2, TGF-β, or both—appears overly simplistic.
While the approach clearly identifies key response elements to these specif-ic immune mediators, it does
not recapitulate the complex immunopathology of IBD as seen in patients.
In line with this, I would have appreciated data derived from the DOGMA-seq platform on mucosal T
cells obtained from IBD patients, both during remission and active disease, or from other immune-
mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs), to strengthen translational relevance.
Finally, I would encourage the authors to reflect on whether their DOGMA-seq platform data provide any
insights into the potential relationship between PGE2 signaling and non-response to anti-TNF therapy,
an important and clinically relevant area that may benefit from the mechanistic resolution their platform
enables.
R: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and constructive comments, and for recognizing
the depth and quality of our T cell characterization. Below, we provide point-by-point responses.
1. We agree with the reviewer that our in vitro model cannot fully recapitulate the complex
mucosal microenvironment of IBD. As clarified in the revised Introduction and Discussion, our
goal was not to simulate the full immunopathology of IBD, but rather to model key aspects of
IBD-relevant immune signaling, focusing on the effects of PGE2, TGF-β, or PGE2 and TGF-β in
T cells that were also exposed to activation stimuli, IL-1β, and IL-23 based on rationales described
in the Introduction and the Discussion.
Importantly, we intentionally used T cells from healthy, young adult donors for several reasons: a)
To avoid confounding effects from immunomodulatory or biologic therapies often used in IBD
and other immune-mediated diseases, which could influence T cell responses in unpredictable
ways; b) To exclude potential confounding from immune aging, ensuring more consistent T cell
biology across donors; c) The age range of our study subjects aligns with the peak onset age for
IBD in adults, improving the relevance of our findings.
Moreover, because there are currently no published single-cell multi-omic datasets focused on
PGE2-mediated changes in T cells from healthy human donors that are also exposed to activation
stimuli, IL-23 and IL-1β, which play key roles in Th17 biology and IBD pathogenesis, our study
provides a necessary and well-controlled foundation for future work on patient samples. While
patient-derived mucosal T cells would indeed further enhance translational relevance, such work
is beyond the scope of the current study. However, we fully recognize its value and plan to pursue
this in future research.
2. We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestion to consider potential links between PGE2
signaling and non-response to anti-TNF therapy2, a clinically important and timely direction. In
our dataset, we observed that TNF expression was significantly downregulated across nearly all
activated T cell subtypes (with the exception of CD4+ regulatory and Gamma Delta cells) upon
PGE2 stimulation. This may reflect a feedback mechanism by which PGE2 suppresses TNF-
mediated effector responses, aligning with its known anti-inflammatory roles in certain contexts.
Furthermore, recent single-cell RNA-seq studies in IBD patients have shown that non-remission
anti-TNF ulcerative colitis patients exhibit elevated expression of IL21, TNFRSF1B, and immune
checkpoint genes (LAG3, CTLA4, TNFRSF4, TNFRSF18, HAVCR2) in Th17 cells3. Using this
gene set, we computed an anti-TNF non-remission module score and found that PGE2-stimulated
Th17 cells consistently showed significantly higher scores in both resting and activated states
(Figure 1A–B; Wilcoxon rank-sum test: P = 0.00014 for resting, P < 2.2×10⁻¹⁶ for activated).
These findings suggest that PGE2 exposure may be associated with poor anti-TNF responsiveness
in Th17 cells.
Figure 1. PGE2 promotes T cell states associated with anti-TNF non-response in Th17 cells.
(A–B) Anti-TNF non-remission module scores (based on IL21, TNFRSF1B, LAG3, CTLA4,
TNFRSF4, TNFRSF18, and HAVCR2) in resting (A) and activated (B) CD4+ memory Th17 cells
under IL-1β/IL-23 stimulation with or without PGE2. Module scores were significantly elevated
in PGE2-stimulated cells in both states (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, P = 0.00014 for resting, P <
2.2×10⁻¹⁶ for activated), indicating a shift toward T cell phenotypes observed in anti-TNF non-
responders.
(C) Drug2cell analysis showing reduced predicted sensitivity to the anti-TNF agent Adalimumab
(CHEMBL1201580) in PGE2-stimulated Th17 cells. Scores reflect enrichment of drug target gene
expression mapped to ADALIMUMAB.
(D) Distribution of Th17 cells in WNN UMAP space under IL-1β/IL-23 stimulation with (orange)
or without (blue) PGE2. Reduced Adalimumab target scores in (C) correspond to the PGE2-
stimulated cluster in (D), supporting a potential link between PGE2 exposure and anti-TNF
resistance phenotypes.
To further explore this hypothesis, we applied Drug2cell4 to score enrichment of anti-TNF target
genes in PGE2-stimulated vs. unstimulated Th17 cells (Figure 1C–D). Using target gene sets for
ADALIMUMAB derived from the ChEMBL database5, we found that PGE2-stimulated Th17
cells exhibited significantly lower drug–target scores, implying reduced predicted sensitivity to
TNF blockade (P = 3.27×10⁻¹⁵, FDR = 2.82×10⁻¹⁴, log₂FC = –1.19). Notably, prior studies have
implicated COX-2–PGE2 signaling in impaired epithelial regeneration and reduced
responsiveness to TNF inhibitors in UC6, consistent with our observations. These findings
reinforce the concept that PGE2 may contribute to treatment resistance in IBD by reprogramming
T cells toward non-responder states. While PGE2 can exert anti-inflammatory effects, its
activation of regulatory pathways in Th17 cells, already implicated in anti-TNF non-response—
raises important considerations for therapeutic strategies.
Given the scope and mechanistic focus of the current study, which centers on mapping PGE2-
mediated chromatin and transcriptional changes, we have opted not to include these findings in
the main text. However, we believe they offer a valuable translational perspective and plan to
explore them further in future patient-focused studies that directly integrate clinical treatment
outcomes.
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful feedback, which has helped us strengthen both the
clarity and translational relevance of our manuscript.
References:
1. Lee J, Aoki T, Thumkeo D, Siriwach R, Yao C, Narumiya S. T cell-intrinsic prostaglandin E(2)-
EP2/EP4 signaling is critical in pathogenic T(H)17 cell-driven inflammation. J Allergy Clin
Immunol 143, 631-643 (2019).
2. Genaro LM, et al. Anti-TNF therapy and immunogenicity in inflammatory bowel diseases: a
translational approach. Am J Transl Res 13, 13916-13930 (2021).
3. Thomas T, et al. A longitudinal single-cell atlas of anti-tumour necrosis factor treatment in
inflammatory bowel disease. Nat Immunol 25, 2152-2165 (2024).
4. Kanemaru K, et al. Spatially resolved multiomics of human cardiac niches. Nature 619, 801-810
(2023).
5. Santos R, et al. A comprehensive map of molecular drug targets. Nat Rev Drug Discov 16, 19-34
(2017).
6. Li Y, et al. COX-2-PGE(2) Signaling Impairs Intestinal Epithelial Regeneration and Associates
with TNF Inhibitor Responsiveness in Ulcerative Colitis. EBioMedicine 36, 497-507 (2018).

### Reviewer 1

Thank you for addressing all comments so completely.
To a large extend the manuscript now reads a lot better.
There is duplication in information now, which should be removed tomorrow improve readability.
All in all the edits have made the goal - method - conclusion of the research much more clear.
The strength in the method used and championed by this manuscript lies in the richness of the information on a single cell level: having communicating layers of RNA, open chromatin and cell surface markers is powerful in itself.
The main issues of the conclusions drawn here are
- based on a limited set of individuals (25) who are healthy (might not be a bad thing, stimulation is controlled which is not the case in diseased individuals, however, we are not well informed whether these stimuli equal disease stimuli)
- specific set of stimuli on which main conclusions are based are only a subset of the total initial study
- conclusion is quite narrow as if this were a hypothesis-p[roving study instead if a hypothesis generating study (which I think it actually is)

### Reviewer 2

The authors clearly respond to all my concerns.

### Reviewer 4

The reviewer notes that the authors have addressed the primary concerns regarding the simplification of their in vitro model and the use of healthy donor T cells. The response appropriately acknowledges that the system does not recapitulate the complex mucosal microenvironment of IBD, and the justification for using healthy donors to avoid confounding from medications, comorbidities, and immune aging is reasonable. The clarifications make it clear that the study is intended as a mechanistic, hypothesis-generating analysis, rather than a definitive model of IBD.
Regarding the potential link between PGE2 signaling and anti-TNF non-response, the authors have provided additional analyses showing that PGE2-stimulated Th17 cells display higher anti-TNF non-remission module scores and reduced predicted sensitivity to Adalimumab using Drug2cell. These analyses, while exploratory and not included in the main text, provide a mechanistic rationale connecting their findings to a clinically relevant phenotype.
However, the manuscript continues to overstate the applicability to IBD, particularly in framing the stimulation conditions as an IBD microenvironment. The data derive from healthy T cells exposed to IL-1β and IL-23 with or without PGE2 (and TGF-
β), which allows for identification of PGE2-specific effects within this context. Nevertheless, the manuscript does not discuss the effects of IL-1β/IL-23 stimulation alone compared to unstimulated controls, nor the combined effect of IL-1β/IL-23/PGE2 versus baseline, leaving a gap in understanding how much of the transcriptional and chromatin changes are attributable to cytokine activation versus PGE2-specific modulation.
The study’s strongest disease-relevant contribution comes from the integration of IBD GWAS SNPs, which serve as a “test case” to prioritize genes and putative regulatory elements. Emphasizing the creation of a large, multimodal T cell resource and its utility in systematically linking genetic risk variants to regulatory programs would better reflect the primary translational contribution, rather than over-interpreting the results as modeling the IBD mucosal microenvironment.
Overall, the authors have satisfactorily addressed the initial concerns regarding the scope and translational interpretation of their work. The manuscript would benefit from reframing to temper disease-specific claims, discussing the baseline effects of cytokine stimulation relative to unstimulated controls (if performed - and if not; a discussion thereof), and highlighting the
DOGMA-seq resource and GWAS integration as the key contributions.

Read the paper and the peer-review interaction below. Based on the scientific concerns raised by the reviewers and the authors' point-by-point response, predict the editorial outcome.
