Then provide a 2–3 sentence rationale explaining your prediction.

## Paper

## Abstract

Genetic and immunologic studies implicate the interleukin (IL)-23/T helper (Th)17 pathway in
inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). IL-23 and IL-1β drive human Th17 differentiation, while
prostaglandin E2 (PGE ) and transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) further modulate Th17
2
development and plasticity. However, how these inflammatory mediators influence human T cell
regulatory programs remains incompletely understood. We used single-cell multi-omics to profile
171,829 peripheral blood T cells from 25 healthy donors in 64 samples exposed to activation
stimuli, IL-1β and IL-23 alone or in combination with PGE , TGF-β, or both. PGE broadly
2 2
suppressed T cell activation, except in Th17 and T follicular helper cells, and markedly altered
chromatin accessibility and gene expression, particularly in Th17, Th1, and regulatory T cells,
where IBD-associated SNPs were enriched in open chromatin and connected to cell type-specific
cis-regulatory elements. Our study demonstrates the utility of single-cell multi-omics for defining
stimulus-specific effects on T cells and prioritizing disease-associated genes.

---

## Introduction

The inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), are
chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disorders of the gastrointestinal tract that affect about
3.7 million people in America and Europe, and hundreds of thousands more globally1-3. The
pathogenesis of IBD is multifactorial, involving both genetic and non-genetic elements such as
environmental factors and gut microbiota2. Further research to unravel the cellular and molecular
mechanisms of IBD is needed for development of more targeted, effective therapies.

Several converging lines of genetic and immunologic evidence suggest that interleukin (IL)-23
signaling and the T helper (Th)17 immune pathway play key roles in the pathogenesis of IBD4-15.
IL-23 and IL-1β drive human Th17 differentiation, and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) and transforming
growth factor-beta (TGF-β) have also been reported to influence Th17 development and/or
plasticity11-13,16-39. These four inflammatory mediators are also overexpressed in IBD tissues40-45,
and genes that encode their receptors (IL23R, IL1R1, and PTGER4) and/or downstream signal
transducers (e.g., TYK2, JAK2, STAT3, SMAD3) are implicated in genome-wide association studies
(GWAS) that have identified thousands of IBD-associated variants4-7.

The strongest association signals in most IBD risk loci lie in non-coding genomic regions where
causal variants cannot be distinguished from neighboring non-causal variants in linkage
disequilibrium, and their presumed cell-type and microenvironment-specific regulatory effects on
gene expression is usually not obvious. Integration of multimodal omics data in disease-relevant
cell types and contexts with epigenetic fine mapping promises to bridge knowledge gaps between
statistical genetic associations and understanding of underlying disease mechanisms46-53.

These rationales motivated us to isolate T cells from the peripheral blood of 25 healthy human
donors with ages 18-35 years, and to expose the T cells to activation stimuli, IL-1β and IL-23 alone
or in combination with PGE2, TGF-β, or both PGE2 and TGF-β to model defined inflammatory
signaling contexts relevant to IBD. By studying T cells from healthy donors with an age range
similar to the peak ages of IBD onset in adults, confounding variables such as IBD-directed
medications, comorbidities, and age-related immune changes that could influence T cell
responses were avoided. The T cells were then profiled using DOGMA-seq, a single-cell trimodal
omics technique incorporating simultaneous assays for gene expression, cell surface protein
epitope antibody-derived tags (ADTs), and the assay for transposase accessible chromatin (ATAC)
within individual cells, enabling higher resolution annotation of specific T cell subtypes and more
robust dissection of complex regulatory networks in comparison to single modal or bimodal
assays54-56.

Leveraging this multimodal omics dataset, we systematically characterized T cell heterogeneity,
quantified PGE2-associated transcriptional and epigenetic changes, and integrated these signals
with IBD GWAS single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to prioritize candidate genes and putative
cis-regulatory elements. Using IBD genetics as a test case, we demonstrated how this resource
can be applied to link disease-associated non-coding variants to cell type-specific regulatory
programs. To validate key findings, we additionally analyzed bulk ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data
from Th17- and Treg-enriched CD4+CD45RO+CD196+ T cells.

In this work, we establish a single-cell multi-omics T cell resource that advances understanding of
how inflammatory cues intersect with genetic risk for IBD. Beyond IBD, this framework provides
a broadly applicable platform for interpreting genetic associations and guiding functional studies
across immune-mediated diseases, including other disorders involving the IL-23/IL-17 pathway,
such as psoriasis and ankylosing spondylitis8,15.

## Results

Simultaneous trimodal single-cell measurement and high-resolution annotation of human
peripheral blood T cells
To characterize the various immune cell states in T cells and the gene regulatory elements in their
subpopulations, we profiled 171,829 high-quality T cells from 25 healthy human donors using
DOGMA-seq (Fig. 1A, Supplementary Fig. 1A). T cells from the first seven study participants were
exposed to anti-CD3/CD28/CD2 activation stimuli, IL-1β and IL-23 (Act IL1B IL23) alone, and in
combination with either PGE2 (Act IL1B IL23 PGE2) or TGF-β (Act IL1B IL23 TGFB), or both PGE2
and TGF-β (Act IL1B IL23 PGE2 TGFB) (7 study participants x 4 conditions), but after we observed
minimal effects of TGF-β (details presented in the Cell type-specific changes upon exposure of T
cells to PGE2 section), cells from the remaining 18 study participants were exposed to just the
conditions without and with PGE2 (Act IL1B IL23 and Act IL1B IL23 PGE2) (18 study participants x
2 conditions), with distinct hashtags added to each of the 64 samples to mitigate batch effects
between samples collected from the same study participant but stimulated differently
(Supplementary Fig. 2A, Supplementary Fig. 1B-C).

We simultaneously assayed 36,601 genes, 163 ADTs, and 252,371 ATAC peaks for each profiled
cell, and this facilitated precise annotation of T cell subpopulations based on canonical markers
in all three modalities (Supplementary Fig. 2B-D). ADTs were particularly effective in
differentiating between CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, and between naïve and memory T cells.
Additionally, ATAC peaks and their associated transcription factor binding motifs57 played a vital
role in identifying T cell subtypes, such as Th1 and Th17 cells.

To address the dynamic changes in T cells upon activation58, we computed activated/resting
scores for each cell based on two lists of signature genes (Fig. 1B, Supplementary Fig. 2E). The
scores are highly correlated with CD25 and CD127 ADTs (Fig. 1C). As both up-regulation of CD25
and down-regulation of CD127 are associated with T cell activation59,60, this finding provides
independent validation of the activated/resting scores. These scores serve as a quantitative proxy
for the continuum of T cell activation states, enabling systematic characterization of activation
heterogeneity across subpopulations61. Leveraging both canonical markers and activated/resting
scores, we identified 20 subtypes of T cells (Fig. 1D, Supplementary Fig. 3), including CD4+ naïve,
CD4+ regulatory, CD4+ memory (further split into four subtypes), CD8+ naïve, CD8+ regulatory,
CD8+ memory, and gamma-delta T cells, and mucosal-associated invariant T cells (MAITs).
Importantly, each cell type is comprised of cells from all study participants, and CD4+ T cells
account for more than half of the T cell population (Supplementary Fig. 1D). These
subpopulations are particularly distinguishable based on ADT and ATAC data (Supplementary Fig.
1E), highlighting the value of multi-omics in comprehensively characterizing T cells.

To further validate the activated/resting scores, an integrative analysis was performed to
combine in-house and public DOGMA-seq data, leveraging the ground truth of T cells treated
with and without anti-CD3/CD28 beads54 (Supplementary Fig. 4A-B). We observed that the
distribution of untreated T cells matches cells with high resting scores from our data, while the
majority of treated T cells overlap with cells exhibiting high activated scores but still contain cells
in the resting state (Supplementary Fig. 4C-D), suggesting that some T cells treated with anti-
CD3/CD28 beads were not fully activated, at least at the time of profiling (16h), or may represent
the lowly active state defined in a recent study58.

Cell type-specific changes upon exposure of T cells to PGE2
When we analyzed 84,345 T cells from seven study participants that were stimulated under four
distinct conditions (Supplementary Fig. 2A, 5B), we observed that the variation between
conditions with and without PGE2 matches the resting and activated states, but we observed
little difference between conditions with and without TGF-β (Supplementary Fig. 5C-D). This
observation is consistent with analysis of data from activated and resting T cells (Supplementary
Fig. 4E). Moreover, we observed significant changes in cell type proportions between conditions
with and without PGE2 but not between conditions with and without TGF-β (Supplementary Fig.
5A). Given these minimal effects of TGF-β, we focused subsequent experiments on two
stimulation conditions, with and without PGE2 (Supplementary Fig. 2A).

Two-sided paired Wilcoxon tests were performed to compare changes in cell type proportions in
129,845 cells from the 25 donors that were stimulated under conditions with and without PGE2.
PGE2 significantly suppresses the activation of multiple T cell subtypes, including CD4+ naïve,
CD4+ regulatory, other CD4+ memory, CD8+ naïve, CD8+ memory, and MAITs (Fig. 2A), which is
consistent with previous reports25. Interestingly, we did not observe immunosuppressive effects
in Th17 and T follicular helper (Tfh) cells.

Differential chromatin accessibility (DA) and differential gene expression (DE) analyses were
performed in 50 paired pseudo-bulk samples (25 study participants x 2 conditions) in each cell
type (Supplementary Data 1-2). While PGE2 suppresses T cell activation, it also up-regulates
numerous ATAC peaks and genes in cells of the resting state, particularly in Th1, Th17, Tfh, and
MAIT cells (Fig. 2B-C). Notably, CREM, STAT4, and PDE4D are among the top up-regulated genes.
Conversely, PTGER4, which encodes the EP4 receptor for PGE2, is strongly down-regulated
(Supplementary Fig. 6-7).

Pathway enrichment analysis reveals that PGE2 exerts opposing effects based on T cell activation
state. Key signaling pathways such as Protein Kinase A (PKA) (including CREM and PDE4D), mTOR,
and JAK/STAT (including STAT4) are up-regulated in resting T cells but down-regulated in
activated T cells (e.g., Th1, other CD4+ memory, CD8+ memory, and MAIT cells), demonstrating
a dual regulatory role (Fig. 2D).

These findings support a model where PGE2 initiates a transient immunomodulatory program via
cAMP–PKA signaling, as evidenced by the up-regulation of CREM and PDE4D62;63. While the
inducible cAMP early repressor isoforms of CREM function as transcriptional repressors of
inflammatory genes, the concurrent up-regulation of PDE4D (which degrades cAMP) and down-
regulation of PTGER4 suggest a negative feedback loop that may prevent prolonged
immunosuppression by self-limiting the signal.

PGE2-induced cAMP has long been recognized for its anti-inflammatory actions64. Interestingly,
while canonical cAMP signaling typically inhibits nuclear factor-kappaB by suppressing IκB kinase
activity65, we observed a noncanonical response in resting Th17 cells, where exposure to PGE2
was associated with transcriptional up-regulation of CREB1, NFKB1, and other cAMP pathway
components, accompanied by increased chromatin accessibility at the NFKB1 locus, suggesting
active transcriptional remodeling. This suggests that cAMP effects may be highly context-
dependent66, and is consistent with murine studies showing that PGE2–EP2/EP4 signaling
cooperates with IL-23 to enhance pathogenic Th17 differentiation67.

In addition, in cells of the resting state, increased activity in the mTOR pathway may reflect
enhanced metabolic preparedness68 and EIF2 pathway up-regulation may indicate translational
reprogramming69.

In parallel, CD4+CD45RO+CD196+ T cells were sorted to enrich Th17 and Treg cells, which were
subsequently activated, stimulated, and subjected to bulk ATAC-seq (cells collected from 33
healthy study participants) and RNA-seq (cells collected from 38 healthy study participants,
Supplementary Fig. 2A). Using bulk samples, CREM, STAT4, PDE4D, and PTGER4 are highlighted
again in DA and DE analyses (Supplementary Fig. 8A, C, Supplementary Data 3-4). To validate
single-cell DA and DE results, we conducted correlative analysis to compare effects observed in
bulk analysis to those observed in comparable single-cell analysis (Supplementary Fig. 8B, D), and
we found high directional concordance. Despite reduced granularity compared to single-cell
analysis (Fig. 2A), bulk analysis still reveals the immunosuppressive effects of PGE2
(Supplementary Fig. 8E).

Allele-specific expression (ASE) and open chromatin (ASoC) analysis reveals stimulation
dependent regulatory dynamics and enrichment in IBD loci
To investigate the impact of stimulation on cis-regulatory variation, we performed ASE and ASoC
analyses in samples from the 25 donors with DOGMA-seq data. ASE refers to the imbalance in
gene expression between two alleles at heterozygous loci, while ASoC reflects allele-specific
differences in chromatin accessibility. High-confidence genotype data for each donor was
obtained directly from the multi-modal single-cell sequencing data by performing germline
variant calling separately from the gene expression and chromatin accessibility modalities of
DOGMA-seq. After discordant variants between RNA- and ATAC-derived SNP calls, flipped alleles
and duplicates, and variants with high missingness were filtered, a total of 60,962 high-
confidence SNPs remained (see Methods for details).

We identified 8,315 significant ASE sites and 18,524 significant ASoC sites (FDR-adjusted P < 0.05)
(Supplementary Data 5-6) Their distribution across each T cell subtype is shown in Supplementary
Fig. 9A. These allele-specific signals are broadly distributed but vary with stimulation condition
and activation state. In the Act IL1B IL23 stimulation condition, activated T cells show a higher
number of significant ASE and ASoC sites than their resting counterparts (paired Wilcoxon rank-
sum P: 2.82x10-3 [ASE] and 3.91x10-3 [ASoC]). However, in the Act IL1B IL23 PGE2 stimulation
condition, this pattern is reversed: resting T cells exhibit significantly more ASoC sites (paired
Wilcoxon rank-sum P: 1.37x10-2), while ASE site numbers are not significantly different (paired
Wilcoxon rank-sum P: 0.213).

To further dissect the impact of PGE2 stimulation, we compared the numbers of significant ASE
and ASoC sites between conditions with and without PGE2 within each T cell subtype, under
otherwise identical stimulation with IL-1β and IL-23. We observe a striking state-dependent
effect. In activated T cells, PGE2 stimulation is associated with a significant reduction in both ASE
and ASoC signals (paired Wilcoxon rank-sum P = 9.77x10⁻³ for both), suggesting dampened allelic
imbalance and potentially reduced regulatory activity under inflammatory conditions. In contrast,
in resting T cells, PGE2 stimulation is associated with a significant increase in the number of both
ASE and ASoC sites (paired Wilcoxon rank-sum P = 1.95x10⁻³), indicating enhanced allele-specific
regulation in the absence of prior activation. These findings further support a model in which
PGE2 exerts inhibitory effects on activated T cells, while promoting greater regulatory
heterogeneity or plasticity in resting T cells. This stimulation-state interaction highlights context-
specific regulatory dynamics of T cells in response to external signals.

While many of the ASE signals are stimulation-specific, a substantial proportion are shared across
all four stimulation conditions, reflecting a stable core of allele-specific regulatory activity.
Specifically, 3,339 ASE variants and 6,198 ASoC variants are consistently detected across all
conditions (Supplementary Fig. 9B–C). In contrast, several hundred sites are unique to individual
conditions, indicating stimulus-specific regulatory effects. Notably, 2,100 variants exhibit
consistent allele-specific signals at both the chromatin and gene expression levels, suggesting
coordinated effects on regulatory architecture.

To evaluate the potential disease relevance of these regulatory variants, we assessed whether
stimulation-responsive ASE and ASoC sites are enriched in genomic regions identified in IBD
GWAS6. Both ASE and ASoC sites show strong enrichment in IBD GWAS loci, highlighting their
potential regulatory involvement in disease susceptibility. This enrichment is most pronounced
for shared sites across all stimulation conditions, but is also evident in stimulation-specific sites.
Specifically, ASE sites show pronounced enrichment with Wilcoxon rank-sum test observed vs.
expected P values of 2.23x10-6 for Act IL1B IL23 PGE2-specific sites, 1.54x10-3 for Act IL1B IL23
TGFB-specific sites, 1.63x10-2 for Act IL1B IL23 PGE2 TGFB-specific sites, 1.78x10-6 for Act IL1B
IL23-specific sites, and 1.53x10-113 for shared sites (Supplementary Fig. 9D). Similarly, ASoC sites
display significant enrichment with P values of 1.62x10-4 for Act IL1B IL23 PGE2-specific sites, 2.90
x10-4 for Act IL1B IL23 TGFB-specific sites, 2.34x10-2 for Act IL1B IL23 PGE2 TGFB-specific sites,
5.62x10-12 for Act IL1B IL23-specific sites, and 2.00x10-199 for shared sites (Supplementary Fig. 9E).
These findings indicate a robust association between ASE and ASoC sites and IBD genetic risk loci,
underscoring the potential functional relevance of these regulatory elements in the pathogenesis
of IBD.

Cell type-specific enrichment of IBD GWAS SNPs in ATAC peaks
Our comprehensively characterized T cell atlas with stratification into activated and resting states
provides an unprecedented opportunity to investigate the T cell subtype specificity of IBD GWAS
SNPs across T cell subpopulations. We focused on 4,329 SNPs from 151 IBD credible sets, which
have a greater than 95% probability of containing the causal variant for each fine-mapped IBD
locus6,70. These variants, hereafter referred to as IBD credible set SNPs, were prioritized based on
Bayesian fine-mapping approaches that account for linkage disequilibrium and effect sizes. The
term 'all variants' refers to the 4,329 IBD SNPs contained within all of the IBD credible sets, while
'lead variants' refers to the 151 IBD SNPs with the most significant GWAS P-value within each IBD
credible set.

To assess cell type-specific enrichment, we used Chromatin Element Enrichment Ranking by
Specificity (CHEERS)71, a statistical method that detects enrichment of disease-associated SNPs
in regulatory regions by accounting for the quantitative, cell-state-specific activity of chromatin
elements. By leveraging the multi-sample design of our study and addressing the sparsity of
single-cell data, we generated 500 pseudo-bulk samples (20 cell types x 25 study participants)
and conducted SNP enrichment analysis using CHEERS, which yielded enrichment P-values for
each pseudo-bulk sample (Supplementary Fig. 10A ). Individual P-values for each cell type were
subsequently combined and adjusted across distinct cell types using the most conservative
methods to narrow down the cell types most worthy of post-GWAS functional investigation (Fig.
3A).

Both lead variants and all variants in the IBD credible set SNPs are strikingly enriched in ATAC
peaks of activated Th17 (Bonferroni-P = 1.36x10-34 [lead] and 3.05x10-30 [all]), Th1 (Bonferroni-P
= 6.64x10-27 [lead] and 3.97x10-19 [all]), and CD4+ Treg cells (Bonferroni-P = 7.75x10-22 [lead] and
1.32x10-7 [all]), reflecting the known dysregulation of the balance between these cell types in IBD
pathogenesis72. In addition, our results also implicate involvement of CD8+ T cells, given the
notable enrichment of lead variants in ATAC peaks of MAITs (Bonferroni-P = 2.78x10-16 [activated]
and 7.76x10-14 [resting]), CD8+ memory (Bonferroni-P = 2.75x10-11 [activated]), and gamma-delta
T cells (Bonferroni-P = 1.10x10-10), which have gained attention in recent studies73,74. Notably,
CD-associated variants show more significant enrichment in activated states, especially in Th17
cells (Bonferroni-P = 1.12x10⁻²⁴ [CD] vs. 9.70x10⁻³ [UC]), suggesting that activated Th17 cells may
play an especially prominent role in CD pathogenesis.

To independently validate these findings, we applied Stratified Linkage Disequilibrium Score
Regression (S-LDSC), a heritability-based method that tests whether GWAS signal is enriched in
specific annotations across these cell types75,76, using IBD, CD, and UC summary statistics6. The
majority of our findings are consistent with those obtained through CHEERS analysis, with
consistent heritability enrichment in activated Th1, Th17, Tfh, CD4+ memory, and Treg cells in
the context of IBD (Fig. 3A).

Notably, a pattern of pronounced heritability enrichment in the activated states of these cells
compared to their resting counterparts emerged from our analysis. This trend is particularly
evident in activated Th1 (Bonferroni-P = 2.74x10-9 [IBD], 2.36x10-6 [CD], 9.20x10-7 [UC]), Th17
(Bonferroni-P = 1.66x10-10 [IBD], 1.37x10-7 [CD], 1.02x10-6 [UC]), Tfh (Bonferroni-P = 4.09x10-5
[IBD], 2.65x10-3 [CD], 1.74x10-3 [UC]), other CD4+ memory (Bonferroni-P = 1.53x10-9 [IBD],
2.03x10-8 [CD], 3.31x10-6 [UC]), and CD4+ Treg cells (Bonferroni-P = 1.41x10-5 [IBD], 2.70x10-6 [CD],
8.15x10-4 [UC]), where significant enrichment is observed across the IBD, CD, and UC phenotypes.

Prostaglandins are involved in diverse biological processes including IBD-related inflammation
and immune responses77, so we next examined whether PGE2 alters enrichment patterns of IBD
risk variants. We generated 480 pseudo-bulk samples (20 cell types x 2 conditions x 12 randomly
selected study participants, Methods) and conducted CHEERS analysis to compare the
enrichment of IBD-associated SNPs in samples stimulated with and without PGE2 (Supplementary
Fig. 10B), followed by combining and adjusting individual P-values (Fig. 3B). The enrichment of
IBD-associated SNPs in cell types is similar to the previous analysis without stratification by
stimulation condition. Specifically, lead variants in the IBD credible set SNPs are significantly
enriched in ATAC peaks of activated Th17 (Bonferroni-P = 5.87x10-27 [w/o PGE2] and 1.34x10-18
[w/ PGE2]), Th1 (Bonferroni-P = 2.21x10-13 [w/o PGE2] and 1.46x10-18 [w/ PGE2]), and CD4+ Treg
cells (Bonferroni-P = 2.56x10-18 [w/o PGE2] and 2.07x10-13 [w/ PGE2]), both with and without
PGE2 stimulation. Interestingly, IBD-associated SNPs show more significant enrichment in resting
Th17 (Bonferroni-P = 1.83x10-15 [w/o PGE2] and 1.05x10-7 [w/ PGE2], difference-P = 6.13x10-3),
other CD4+ memory (Bonferroni-P = 3.62x10-5 [w/o PGE2] and 1 [w/ PGE2], difference-P =
1.89x10-4), and CD8+ memory T cells (Bonferroni-P = 8.64x10-6 [w/o PGE2] and 1 [w/ PGE2],
difference-P = 8.64x10-4) without PGE2 stimulation, despite their lower cell type proportions in
the absence of PGE2 stimulation. In contrast, IBD-associated SNPs show more significant
enrichment in activated CD8+ memory T cells (Bonferroni-P = 9.67x10-9 [w/o PGE2] and 4.84x10-
17 [w/ PGE2], difference-P = 1.53x10-2) upon PGE2 stimulation.

Differences in enrichment between conditions with and without PGE2 are relatively modest for
CD-associated SNPs, with significance detected only in resting MAITs (difference-P = 7.69x10-3
[lead] and 1.58x10-2 [all]), compared with those for UC-associated SNPs, suggesting that PGE2
differentially modulates chromatin accessibility at CD- and UC-associated risk loci. Notably, this
aligns with clinical observations that non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use, which is
known to reduce endogenous PGE2 levels, is associated with increased relapse risk in CD but not
UC78. Our findings suggest a possible mechanism: the reduced regulatory flexibility at CD risk loci
could increase vulnerability to PGE2 depletion during NSAID exposure, whereas the
comparatively greater plasticity of UC loci may help buffer against such effects.

Cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages facilitating annotation of ATAC peaks and
identification of plausible cis-regulatory elements (CREs)
To better understand the regulatory function of non-coding chromatin regions, we identified
peak-to-gene linkages, which are correlations between chromatin accessibility peaks and
expression levels of nearby genes, thereby mapping candidate CREs to their putative gene
targets79. We initially used ArchR, a computational framework that enables scalable inference of
peak-to-gene regulatory relationships from single-cell data to identify peak-to-gene linkages
within a distance of 1 Mb for T cell subpopulations80. To improve robustness, we refined the
initial linkages from ArchR by validating them using pseudo-bulk correlation analyses, generating
64 pseudo-bulk samples for each cell type.

This analysis yielded an average of 101,972 plausible peak-to-gene linkages for each
subpopulation (Fig. 3C), constituting approximately 6.5% of peak-to-gene linkages initially
discovered using ArchR (Methods). On average, 76.1% (ranging from 60.6% to 90.9%) of plausible
peak-to-gene linkages were confirmed as positive associations. Notably, these results reveal that
regulatory interactions are highly cell type-specific and often extend beyond nearest-gene
assumptions. Only 8.5% (ranging from 4.4% to 14.0%) of the top linked genes were found to be
the nearest genes to their corresponding ATAC peaks (Fig. 3D), emphasizing the need to go
beyond proximity-based annotations when assigning regulatory elements to target genes.
Interestingly, we found that both CD4+ and CD8+ naïve T cells have fewer linked peaks and genes
(Fig. 3E-F), suggesting a more transcriptionally quiescent or less differentiated regulatory state
despite their high abundance. Linked peaks and genes shared between different cell types are
summarized in Supplementary Fig. 11A-B.

Together, these regulatory maps offer valuable insights into the functional annotation of non-
coding chromatin regions. By linking T cell subtype-specific chromatin accessibility peaks that
overlap disease-associated SNPs with downstream gene targets, they help clarify cellular
contexts in which disease-associated SNPs may exert pathogenic effects.

SCARlink reveals putative enhancers and supports regulatory interpretations of peak-to-gene
linkages
We applied SCARlink, a computational method that predicts enhancer-gene relationships using
joint single-cell gene expression and chromatin accessibility profiles, to augment understanding
of cis-regulatory mechanisms and annotation of enhancer elements relevant to IBD in T cells81.
SCARlink fits a regularized Poisson regression to predict single-cell gene expression based on
accessibility of fixed-size genomic tiles and calculates cell type-specific Shapley values, which
quantify the relative importance of each tile in explaining the expression of a given gene.
Genomic regions with high Shapley values are prioritized as candidate enhancers in a cell-type-
specific manner.

SCARlink was applied to 5,000 highly variable genes (HVGs) identified in DOGMA-seq data. Genes
with sparse expression (defined as having more than 90% zero values) were excluded, resulting
in a final set of 1,256 genes for analysis. Across all T-cell subpopulations, we identified an average
of 38,819 significant gene-linked tiles per subpopulation (ranging from 9,235 to 100,313) linked
to 1,247 genes on average (ranging from 1,209 to 1,254) after FDR adjustment. Importantly,
SCARlink also provided independent support for 4,916 peak-to-gene linkages per subtype (range:
1,130–11,075), based on the colocalization of predicted enhancer tiles within or overlapping
previously linked ATAC peaks. These results suggest that a substantial proportion of peak-to-gene
relationships may be mechanistically driven by cell type-specific enhancer activity.

The full set of SCARlink predictions provided in Supplementary Data 7 serve as a high-resolution,
cell-type-resolved map of putative enhancers in human T cells and provide mechanistic insights
into how noncoding variation at ATAC peaks may influence gene expression.

Cell type-specific colocalization of IBD-associated SNPs in plausible CREs
Next, we conducted a colocalization analysis to identify ATAC peaks that are both associated with
cis-gene expression (plausible CREs) and overlap all or lead IBD credible set SNPs, thereby
revealing the enrichment of IBD credible set SNPs in specific loci and prioritizing cell types crucial
to disease pathogenesis.

Focusing on the cell types prioritized by CHEERS and S-LDSC, all variants were found to be
strikingly enriched in peaks linked to PTGER4 (Fig. 4A). For instance, the ATAC peak chr5-
40490646-40491146, covering the SNP rs10440635 (Fig. 4B), displays significant positive
association with PTGER4 across seven distinct cell types, including activated and resting CD4+
naïve T, resting CD4+ Treg, activated Th1, resting Th17 and Tfh, and activated CD8+ naïve T cells
(Supplementary Fig. 12A). SCARlink analysis reveals that the predicted PTGER4 gene expression
shows a Spearman correlation R² of 0.244 (Supplementary Fig. 13), well above the genome-wide
average of 0.116, indicating that chromatin accessibility is a major determinant of PTGER4
expression in T cells and may mediate genetic risk for IBD. We identified a significant PTGER4-
linked tile (chr5-40490500-40491000) through Shapley value analysis and expression prediction
testing that overlaps both rs10440635 and the peak chr5-40490646-40491146 in five T cell
subtypes including resting and activated CD4⁺ naïve, activated Th1, resting Th17, and activated
CD8⁺ naïve T cells, supporting the presence of a cell type-specific enhancer that may regulate
PTGER4 and contribute to IBD pathogenesis (Supplementary Fig. 13 and Supplementary Data 8).
Of note, rs10440635 not only resides within the IBD credible set spanning from 40486896 to
40623346 on chr570 but it has also been implicated in ankylosing spondylitis, a condition closely
linked with IBD, and is presumed to regulate the expression of PTGER4 in synovial biopsies82.
Although not reported among 216,597 immune cell type-specific cis-expression quantitative trait
loci (eQTL) identified in single-cell eQTL analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells83,
rs10440635 was a PTGER4 eQTL in eQTLGen data84 from blood (P = 2.02x10-8) and achieved
nominal significance in GTEx data85 from EBV-transformed lymphocytes (Supplementary Fig. 12B),
thereby highlighting the need for eQTL analysis with finer granularity to verify this plausible
association.

Similarly, another 12 IBD-associated SNPs are covered by an additional 10 ATAC peaks that are
correlated with PTGER4 across 13 subtypes of T cells (Supplementary Fig. 12A), including
rs9292781 and rs1122433 that map within chr5-40578427-40578927 (Fig. 4B), and were both
PTGER4 eQTLs in eQTLGen data84 from blood (P = 4.77x10-25 and 4.42x10-30). The tile chr5-
40578500-40579000, which includes rs1122433, is significantly linked to PTGER4 and overlaps
the peak-to-gene linkage between PTGER4 and chr5-40578427-40578927 in activated and
resting CD4+ naïve, activated CD8+ naïve, activated Th1, and other activated CD4+ memory T
cells, suggesting an additional enhancer region that may contribute to PTGER4 regulation and
IBD risk (Supplementary Data 8). These findings converge on the PTGER4 locus as a genetically
and epigenetically regulated target in T cells, strongly implicating PGE2–EP4 signaling in IBD
pathogenesis.

Other colocalized SNP–CRE relationships were also identified. Around LNPEP, a gene that has
received little attention in the context of IBD despite evidence indicating a decrease in its serum
protein abundance in CD patients86, 35 IBD-associated SNPs fall within 14 peaks correlated with
LNPEP expression across 16 cell types (Supplementary Fig. 14A, 15). Interestingly, the ATAC peak
chr5-96896251-96896751 covers eight IBD-associated SNPs and is a plausible CRE for LNPEP in
eight cell types (Supplementary Fig. 14B). Analysis of all variants also reveals enrichment in linked
peaks for TNFRSF14 (e.g., rs2227313 in resting CD8+ naïve T cells and six other cell types, which
was also revealed as a single-cell eQTL in multiple T cell subpopulations83, Supplementary Fig. 16-
17), and IL2RA (e.g., rs61839660, which has a posterior probability of 0.999 to be a causal variant
for CD70 in activated CD4+ and CD8+ naïve T cells, Supplementary Fig. 18-19). From SCARlink
analysis, we found that IL2RA gene expression is strongly predicted by chromatin accessibility
(Spearman R² = 0.511) and is associated with the predicted enhancer tile chr10:6052500–
6053000, which covers rs61839660 across four cell types (Supplementary Fig. 20 and
Supplementary Data 9).

In comparison, analysis of lead variants uncovered the highest number of overlaps between IBD-
associated SNPs and CREs governing CCL20 and CXCR5. For instance, rs1811711, with a posterior
probability of 0.914 for being a causal variant for UC but not directly linked to CCL20 in a previous
fine mapping study6, was identified within a plausible CRE correlated with CCL20 expression in
activated Tfh cells and seven other cell types (Supplementary Fig. 21A-B). The association
between rs1811711 and CCL20 was further supported by eQTL data from whole blood
(Supplementary Fig. 21C). Similarly, rs630923, with a posterior probability of 0.820 for being a
causal variant for CD but not directly linked to CXCR5 in a previous fine mapping study70, was
identified within a plausible CRE correlated with CXCR5 expression in activated other CD4+
memory T cells and another five cell types (Supplementary Fig. 22A-B), although the association
between rs630923 and CXCR5 hasn’t been revealed by published bulk and single-cell eQTL
analyses.

These colocalization analyses provide not only specific loci but also cell-type specificity of IBD-
associated SNPs, compared to the general enrichment pattern revealed by CHEERS and S-LDSC.
Moreover, the colocalization of IBD-associated SNPs within cell type-specific CREs provides
compelling evidence for the association between genes regulated by CREs and SNPs located
within those CREs. The integration of SCARlink results further strengthens this analysis by
providing detailed predictions of gene-linked tiles and identifying potential enhancer elements
that regulate gene expression. This relationship is not fully elucidated by existing bulk and single-
cell eQTL analyses, highlighting the importance of in-depth, cell type-specific investigations with
greater precision. Together, these findings offer mechanistic insights into how genetic variants
may influence cell type-specific regulatory programs that contribute to IBD pathogenesis.

Cell type-specific colocalization of IBD-associated SNPs, DA peaks, peak-to-gene linkages, and
DE genes
To investigate the impact of both genetic and inflammatory factors (PGE2) on immune
dysregulation in IBD87, a colocalization analysis was performed to connect IBD-associated SNPs
with DA peaks and DE genes between T cell stimulation conditions with and without PGE2
(Supplementary Data 10). We hypothesized that ATAC peaks correlated with gene expression and
covering SNPs may be CREs that are potentially impacted by genetic susceptibility. Furthermore,
if these peaks and their linked genes are also altered upon PGE2 stimulation, this could suggest
a pathway that is potentially involved in IBD pathogenesis.

Out of the 151 IBD credible sets, 72 contain 633 IBD-associated SNPs involved in colocalization
events (Supplementary Data 11-12), marking a subset of these credible sets as essential for
exploring immune dysregulation in IBD influenced by both genetic and inflammatory factors.
Moreover, these events implicate a total of 325 genes, shedding light on critical pathways,
including the IL-2 signaling pathway, Th1 cytokine production, and NK cell differentiation
(Supplementary Data 13).

The greatest number of colocalization events cluster around PTGER4, highlighting 17 events
across seven T cell subsets. For example, rs10440635 is located within the ATAC peak chr5-
40490646-40491146, which is altered by PGE2 and correlated with the DE gene PTGER4. Such
associations are consistent across multiple T cell subsets, including activated CD4+ naïve, Th1,
CD8+ naïve, and resting CD4+ naïve T cells (Fig. 5A). These observations are further supported by
bulk data analysis from cells enriched for Th17 and Treg cells (Fig. 5B). As mentioned in the former
section, rs10440635 is located within a plausible CRE regulating PTGER4 expression across seven
distinct cell types. The additional findings that both the CRE's activity and PTGER4 expression are
modulated by PGE2 in a subset of these cells— four out of the seven T cell types— further
emphasize their plausible role in IBD pathogenesis. Similarly, we observed that rs9292781 and
rs1122433 are colocalized with a DA peak and the DE gene PTGER4 across four T cell subtypes
(Fig. 5C), with validation in bulk data (Fig. 5D). Collectively, our findings strikingly highlight
rs10440635, rs9292781, and rs1122433 for their pivotal roles in modulating PTGER4 expression
through the CREs where they reside across activated CD4+ naïve, Th1, CD8+ naïve, and resting
CD4+ naïve T cells, and this is further supported by validation with Hi-C data from GM12878 cell
lines88,89 (Supplementary Fig. 23A-C). This regulation, in conjunction with their responses to PGE2
stimulation, is particularly compelling, given PGE2's capacity to directly bind to the EP4 receptor
encoded by PTGER4, thereby delineating a mechanistic link to IBD pathogenesis.

Our colocalization analysis also highlights SNPs around SATB1 (10 events across four
subpopulations, Supplementary Fig. 24A-B), which regulate the pathogenic function of Th17 cells
in the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis model for multiple sclerosis90, and intestinal
epithelial function91. Additionally, SNPs around GPR183 (Supplementary Fig. 24C-D) and
RASGRP1 (Supplementary Fig. 24E) are highlighted. GPR183 expression is increased in the
presence of the CC allele of another IBD-associated SNP, rs9557195, and on lymphocytes
expressing chemokine receptors CCR6 or CCR9 and Th17 cells92. On the other hand, decreased
RASGRP1 in CD4+ T cells is correlated with active inflammation, while deletion of RASGRP1 causes
defective T lymphocyte development93. These findings are consistent with findings in our bulk
data. Interestingly, colocalization events for SNPs around CREM (a top up-regulated gene upon
PGE2 stimulation across various T cell subpopulations) are identifiable only in our single-cell
analyses of specific T cell subtypes but not bulk data (Supplementary Fig. 24F). These prioritized
IBD-associated SNPs around SATB1, GPR183, RASGRP1, and CREM also showed significant
associations with lymphocyte or eosinophil counts94, which could be substantially influenced by
PGE2 stimulation. This convergence of genetic and inflammatory factors underlines the complex
interplay in IBD pathogenesis.

Valuable resource for investigating other immune-mediated inflammatory diseases
Beyond prioritizing IBD credible sets and T cell subpopulations, our comprehensively
characterized T cell atlas can be generalized as a versatile resource to investigate other immune-
mediated inflammatory diseases. Similar to the enrichment of IBD GWAS SNPs in ATAC peaks,
we
examined 4,950 fine-mapped SNPs associated with 21 immune-mediated diseases, nearly all of
which are preferentially mapped to enhancers and promoters active in CD4+ T cells51, using
CHEERS. This analysis yielded enrichment P-values for each of the 500 pseudo-bulk sample
(Supplementary Fig. 25A) that were subsequently combined and adjusted as above
(Supplementary Fig. 25B).

We found that CD8+ memory T cells, both in resting and activated states, show striking
enrichment for disease-associated SNPs across multiple disorders, particularly psoriasis, Behçet’s
disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). For example, we found a striking enrichment
of psoriasis-associated SNPs in ATAC peaks of CD8+ memory cells, with remarkably low
Bonferroni-adjusted P-values (Bonferroni-P) of 2.17x10-49 (resting state) and 1.37x10-45 (activated
state). This finding was not reported in the earlier fine mapping study51. CD8+ T cells have
subsequently been recognized as key effector cells and the predominant intra-epidermal T cells
in psoriatic plaques, and neutralization of CD8+ T cells prevents the development of psoriasis in
a xenograft model95. We also observed a notable enrichment of Behçet's disease-associated SNPs
in resting (Bonferroni-P = 4.18x10-43) and activated (Bonferroni-P = 7.86x10-39) CD8+ memory T
cell ATAC peaks. The frequency of CD8+ T cells is increased in patients with active Behçet's
disease and HLA-B51, and knock-out of ERAP1 in the presence of HLA-B51 alters CD8 T cell
immunity96.

In addition, we found that alopecia areata-associated SNPs are enriched in activated CD4+
regulatory T cells (Treg, Bonferroni-P = 1.33x10-37) ATAC peaks. Treg in hair follicles can facilitate
hair follicle regeneration by promoting hair follicle stem cell proliferation and differentiation97,
and Treg augmentation using low-dose IL-2 is an effective treatment98. We found that ankylosing
spondylitis-associated SNPs are enriched in resting (Bonferroni-P = 3.85x10-35) and activated
(Bonferroni-P = 7.27x10-30) CD8+ memory T cells, which can be primed by microbial peptides
presented by HLA-B27 and subsequently interact with self-peptides that HLA-B27 can bind99.
Furthermore, SLE-associated SNPs are enriched in activated CD8+ memory T cell ATAC peaks
(Bonferroni-P = 2.53x10-31). Defective effector CD8+ T cell function in SLE leads to failure to
remove autoreactive B cells that induce autoimmunity100.

Colocalization analysis of immune-mediated disease SNPs within cell type-specific CREs also
prioritize genetic loci and cell types crucial to disease pathogenesis. Focusing on the ten cell types
prioritized by CHEERS, psoriasis-associated SNPs were found to be enriched in peaks linked to
IFNLR1 (Supplementary Fig. 26A), as well as RUNX3 (Supplementary Fig. 27A) expression. In
psoriasis, Th17-secreted IL-29 mediates cutaneous anti-viral competence by activating IFNLR1101,
and we found that eight psoriasis-associated SNPs around IFNLR1 fall within five peaks correlated
with IFNLR1 expression across nine cell types (Supplementary Fig. 26B), involving both proximal
(e.g., rs7552167 in resting Th17 cells) and distal (e.g., rs11249213, rs4265380, and rs7414934 in
gamma-delta T cells) regulation of IFNLR1 expression. RUNX3 is important for CD8+ T cell
development and the differentiation of Th1 and Th17 cells102, and we found that ten psoriasis-
associated SNPs around RUNX3 fall within four peaks correlated with RUNX3 expression across
nine cell types (Supplementary Fig. 27B), involving both proximal (e.g., rs11249213, rs4265380,
and rs7414934 in resting Th1 cells) and distal (e.g., rs4090311 and rs78312791 in resting Th17
cells) regulation of RUNX3 expression. We also observed that Behcet’s disease-associated SNPs
are enriched in peaks correlated with KLRC4 expression (e.g., rs1841957 and rs1841958 in resting
CD8+ memory T cells, Supplementary Fig. 28A-B). Other notable associations include enrichment
of alopecia areata SNPs near IL21 in Th1 cells, ankylosing spondylitis SNPs near GPR65 in MAITs,
and SLE SNPs near BLK and CD44 in CD8+ memory T cells (Supplementary Fig. 29–32).

These results collectively highlight the broader applicability of our T cell atlas for elucidating
regulatory mechanisms across diverse immune-mediated diseases. In particular, the
convergence of genetic enrichment in CD8+ memory T cells across multiple conditions suggests
shared effector pathways that may underlie common immunopathology and provides a
foundation for therapeutic hypothesis generation across a spectrum of inflammatory disorders.
