Comments on the Introduction
The introduction is largely appropriate until the paragraph beginning with "Thus, to further elucidate."
Some issues arise at this point:
• It is not clearly stated what types of T cells were used, nor how they were prepared.
• DOGMA-seq is introduced abruptly without even a short definition. A brief one-sentence
explanation could help (e.g., "DOGMA-seq enables simultaneous profiling of chromatin, transcriptomics,
and surface proteins in single cells.").
• There is no transition explaining why single-cell multi-omics is necessary for this study. One
linking sentence could greatly improve clarity.
• PGE2 is introduced without sufficient background on its relevance to T cell biology or IBD.
Suggestions:
• Add 1–2 bridging sentences clarifying why DOGMA-seq was necessary and why PGE2 was
studied.
• Soften overly enthusiastic language about the methods; let the value of the approach emerge
naturally from the results.
R: In the revised Introduction, we explicitly state that we studied T cells isolated from the peripheral blood
of healthy human donors with ages 18-35 years, an age range similar to the peak ages of IBD onset in
adults. The relevance of PGE2 and the other inflammatory mediators in the T cell stimulation cocktails to
T cell biology and IBD is discussed. DOGMA-seq is introduced as a single-cell trimodal omics technique
incorporating simultaneous assays for gene expression, cell surface protein epitope antibody-derived tags,
and the assay for transposase accessible chromatin within individual cells, enabling higher resolution
annotation of specific T cell subtypes and more robust dissection of complex regulatory networks in
comparison to single modal or bimodal assays. Overly enthusiastic language about the methods has been
deleted.
Results: Simultaneous trimodal measurement and annotation of human peripheral blood T cells
This section contains important information, but there are areas where the writing could be made much
clearer:
• The rationale for PGE2 stimulation remains unclear. Even a single sentence explaining that PGE2
is elevated in IBD and modulates immune responses would help set expectations.
• The switch from four stimulation conditions to two is confusing and should be explained more
simply ("Minimal effects were observed with TGF-β, so subsequent experiments focused on PGE2
alone.").
• There is too much technical detail about DOGMA-seq in the Results section; this could be
streamlined to keep the focus on biological findings.
• The relevance of the activated/resting scores could be better framed to explain biological meaning,
not just statistical validation.
• Some apparent paradoxes (e.g., overall suppression of activation markers yet upregulation of
pathways like mTOR and STAT4) are not explained.
Suggestions:
• Briefly frame PGE2 relevance upfront.
• Explain design choices (4 vs 2 stimulation conditions) cleanly.
• Streamline technical descriptions to avoid distracting from main findings.
• Clarify the biological relevance of the activation/resting comparisons.
R: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful comments and suggestions regarding the Results section. We
have carefully revised the text to improve clarity and to better explain the rationale, design decisions, and
biological interpretation of our findings.
1. The relevance of PGE2 and the other inflammatory mediators in the T cell stimulation cocktails
to T cell biology and IBD is discussed in the Introduction.
2. We have clarified the stimulation design. Specifically, we now explain that we initially
evaluated four stimulation conditions but observed minimal effects of TGF-β, so we focused
subsequent experiments on PGE2 by comparing two conditions with or without PGE2.
3. To maintain focus on biological insights, we have streamlined the technical details in the Results
section. Methodological aspects such as the calculation of activated/resting scores, pseudo-bulk
construction, and DOGMA-seq data processing are now described in the Methods section only.
This allows the Results to more directly emphasize key biological findings.
4. In response to the suggestion for better framing of the activated/resting comparisons, we now
describe the biological relevance of this dichotomy. Specifically, we show that while PGE2
broadly suppresses T cell activation across multiple subtypes, including CD4+ naïve, CD4+
regulatory, CD4+ memory, CD8+ naïve, CD8+ memory, and MAIT cells, it also induces
upregulation of numerous genes in resting T cells, including CREM, STAT4, and PDE4D, along
with activation of Protein Kinase A (PKA), mTOR, EIF2, and IL-23–related signaling pathways.
In contrast, these same pathways are down-regulated in activated cells, particularly in Th1, CD4+
memory, CD8+ memory, and MAIT cells.
We now provide a mechanistic interpretation of this pattern. PGE2 may initiate a transient
immunomodulatory program via the cAMP–PKA axis, while also engaging a negative feedback
loop through upregulation of PDE4D (which degrades cAMP) and downregulation of PTGER4
and the EP4 receptor for PGE2 that PTGER4 encodes, preventing prolonged immunosuppression.
Simultaneously, we observe upregulation of STAT4 related pathways in resting T cells, suggesting
that resting T cells may be transcriptionally primed for cytokine-driven differentiation.
The suppression of T cell activation and upregulation of pathways such as mTOR and STAT4
reflect dual and context-specific roles of PGE2. In resting cells, these pathways may promote
metabolic readiness and selective transcriptional priming, whereas in activated cells, they are
down-regulated, possibly due to exhaustion, desensitization, or dominance of TCR-driven
programs.
Additionally, we now include new observations related to Th17 cells, where we detect a
noncanonical transcriptional response. Upon PGE2 stimulation, CREB1, NFKB1, and other
cAMP-related genes are upregulated in resting Th17 cells. Chromatin accessibility also increases
near the NFKB1 locus, suggesting transcriptional remodeling. These findings are consistent with
prior murine studies showing that PGE2–EP2/EP4 signaling can synergize with IL-23 to enhance
Th17 pathogenic programs via CREB1, STAT3, and NF-κB1. We interpret this as further evidence
of the flexible, context-dependent reprogramming induced by PGE2.
Results: Allele-specific expression (ASE) and open chromatin (ASoC) analyses
The ASE/ASoC analysis is very valuable but quite difficult to follow:
• The section opens with technical steps (germline variant calling, discordant variants) without
stating why this matters — a short framing sentence would help.
• ASE and ASoC abbreviations are heavily used without reminding the reader what they mean.
• Wilcoxon P-values are reported, but their biological meaning is not interpreted.
• Excessive enumeration of SNP counts and condition-specific sites makes it hard to retain the
main point.
• The final, very important finding — that ASE and ASoC sites are enriched in IBD loci — is
somewhat buried.
Suggestions:
• Briefly explain the goal of the ASE/ASoC quality control at the beginning.
• Re-introduce ASE and ASoC definitions clearly.
• Interpret the biological meaning of increased/decreased ASE and ASoC after PGE2 stimulation.
• Emphasize the enrichment in IBD loci more clearly and earlier in the paragraph.
R: We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments about the ASE/ASoC section. We have revised
the text substantially to improve clarity, structure, and biological interpretation.
1. We now begin the section with a concise statement outlining the purpose of the ASE and ASoC
analyses and the rationale for initial variant-level quality control. We explain that we performed
germline variant calling separately from the gene expression and chromatin accessibility
modalities of DOGMA-seq, allowing us to infer sample-matched genotypes without requiring
external genotyping arrays, and then filtered discordant variants between RNA- and ATAC-
derived SNP calls, flipped alleles and duplicates, and variants with high missingness to arrive at
high confidence genotype calls for accurate and allele-consistent integration of chromatin
accessibility and gene expression data. This provides biological context for the technical
description that follows. We have moved all details regarding proportions and numbers of
identified SNPs except the total number of high-confidence SNPs that remained to the Methods
section.
2. To improve readability, after defining abbreviations for allele-specific expression (ASE) and
open chromatin (ASoC) when first mentioned in the Introduction, we have reintroduced these
definitions again in the title of the Results subsection where ASE and ASoC analyses are presented.
(We have also re-introduced abbreviations for differential chromatin accessibility (DA) and gene
expression (DE) a few times throughout the manuscript, and we have provided an additional table
for abbreviations in the supplementary files.)
3. We have added biological interpretation of the Wilcoxon test results. Specifically, we highlight
that the increased number of significant ASE and ASoC sites in resting versus activated T cells
after exposure to PGE2 suggests enhanced allele-specific regulation in the resting state, consistent
with our previous findings that PGE2 suppresses activation programs while maintaining or even
enhancing transcriptional and epigenetic plasticity in resting T cells. Conversely, the reduction of
ASE and ASoC sites in activated cells under PGE2 stimulation suggests an inhibitory effect on
transcriptional complexity or regulatory heterogeneity in an already activated state. These
biological interpretations are now stated clearly alongside the statistical comparisons.
4. In response to the concern about excessive enumeration, we have reduced the number of exact
SNP counts presented in the main text and moved detailed breakdowns to the Supplementary
Tables and Figures. The main paragraph now focuses on the key patterns and biological
implications of stimulation-specific versus shared allele-specific regulation.
5. Finally, and importantly, we have revised the structure of the section so that the enrichment of
ASE and ASoC sites in IBD GWAS loci, a central result of this analysis, is presented earlier and
more prominently. We now emphasize this finding as a major conclusion of the section,
highlighting its relevance for understanding the genetic architecture of IBD and the stimulation-
dependent regulatory landscape of human T cells.
We hope these changes improve the clarity and impact of this section in line with the reviewer’s helpful
suggestions.
Results: Enrichment of IBD GWAS SNPs in ATAC peaks
The general structure of this section is logical, but it can be improved:
• "Credible SNPs" should be defined briefly when first mentioned.
• CHEERS and S-LDSC are introduced without explaining their purposes in simple terms.
• P-values are listed in dense groups without summarizing the overall patterns or trends.
• Some key biological implications, particularly about activated T cell subtypes mediating IBD
risk, are understated.
• The relevance of PGE2 shifting enrichment patterns is interesting but could be better linked to
clinical observations (e.g., NSAID effects in Crohn's vs UC).
Suggestions:
• Add short, plain-language explanations of credible SNPs, CHEERS, and S-LDSC.
• Summarize biological conclusions first before presenting detailed statistics.
• Conclude the section with a clear statement about the clinical relevance of these findings.
R: We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback. In the revised manuscript, we have made several
changes to improve clarity, interpretation, and clinical relevance in this section:
1. We now define “IBD credible set SNPs” at the point they are first mentioned. We explain that
these SNPs were prioritized based on Bayesian fine-mapping approaches that account for linkage
disequilibrium and effect size, and are comprised of the SNPs in each of 151 fine-mapped IBD
loci which have a greater than 95% probability of containing the causal variant.
2. To aid understanding of the analytical tools used, we have added concise explanations for both
CHEERS and S-LDSC. We describe CHEERS as a method that detects enrichment of disease-
associated SNPs in regulatory regions by accounting for the quantitative, cell-state-specific
activity of chromatin elements. We describe our application of S-LDSC as a heritability-based
method that tests whether GWAS signal is enriched in specific annotations across cell types.
3. We have restructured the paragraph to present biological conclusions first, followed by
supporting statistics. For example, we now summarize that IBD SNPs are most strongly enriched
in activated Th17, Th1, and CD4+ Treg cells, and that CD-associated SNPs show stronger
enrichment in activated states than UC-associated SNPs, before detailing the exact P-values.
4. We have expanded our interpretation of biological trends, emphasizing the prominent role of
activated CD4+ T cell subsets (Th1, Th17, CD4+ Treg) across both CHEERS and S-LDSC results,
which supports their key involvement in IBD pathogenesis.
5. To address the reviewer’s final point, we have revised the last paragraph of the section to
explicitly link PGE2-dependent enrichment pattern shifts to clinical observations that NSAID use,
which is known to reduce endogenous PGE2 levels, is associated with increased relapse risk in
CD but not UC. We state that reduced regulatory flexibility at CD risk loci could increase
vulnerability to PGE2 depletion during NSAID exposure, whereas the comparatively greater
plasticity of UC loci may help buffer against such effects.
We believe these revisions significantly enhance the clarity, biological insight, and translational relevance
of the section and hope they adequately address the reviewer’s concerns.
Results: Cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages
This section is important but could be made easier to follow:
• "Peak-to-gene linkage" should be briefly explained for readers less familiar with single-cell
analysis.
• The use of ArchR is introduced without explaining its role.
• Again, the biological interpretation of the findings should come before listing numbers.
• A short closing statement explaining why this matters (e.g., better annotation of non-coding
disease variants) would strengthen the section.
Suggestions:
• Add short intuitive definitions and interpretations before presenting numbers.
• End the section by framing why these regulatory maps are important for understanding IBD
genetics.
R: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful comments and suggestions regarding the clarity and
interpretability of this important section. In the revised manuscript, we have made several changes to
address these points:
1. We have added a brief, intuitive definition of peak-to-gene linkages early in the section,
explaining that they are correlations between chromatin accessibility peaks and expression levels
of nearby genes, thereby mapping candidate cis-regulatory elements (CREs) to their putative gene
targets.
2. We clarified the role of ArchR as a computational framework for inferring peak-to-gene linkages
from single-cell multi-omic data.
3. To improve readability, we restructured the paragraph so that biological insights appear before
the detailed numerical results. Specifically, we first highlight that peak-to-gene linkages often
reveal regulatory relationships beyond nearest-gene assignments, and that naïve T cells tend to
have fewer such linkages despite their abundance, indicating lower regulatory complexity in their
resting states.
4. Finally, we added a closing sentence emphasizing the significance of these regulatory maps for
IBD genetics. We state that identifying cell type-specific peak-to-gene linkages enables more
accurate annotation of non-coding disease variants, and provides mechanistic hypotheses linking
GWAS loci to gene regulation in relevant T cell subsets.
We believe these revisions improve the accessibility and biological interpretation of the section and thank
the reviewer again for helping to strengthen this part of the manuscript.
Results: SCARlink predictions
While SCARlink is a strong addition to the study, it is not well introduced:
• Shapley values are mentioned without explaining what they mean in this context.
• The SCARlink method workflow is not clearly outlined.
• The biological relevance to enhancer prediction for IBD is not made explicit.
• Too many raw numbers are listed before any interpretation.
Suggestions:
• Introduce Shapley values with one sentence explaining the concept intuitively.
• Briefly describe the goal of SCARlink (predicting enhancers linked to gene expression).
• State the biological relevance upfront before listing numbers.
R: We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. In the revised manuscript, we clarify the goal of
SCARlink at the beginning of the section by explicitly stating that it predicts enhancer-gene relationships
using single-cell gene expression and chromatin accessibility data. We also introduce Shapley values as a
measure of the relative importance of fixed-size genomic tiles in explaining the expression of a given gene.
To improve readability, we mention the biological rationale for applying SCARlink, to augment
understanding of cis-regulatory mechanisms and annotation of enhancer elements relevant to IBD in T
cells, earlier in the section. Finally, we have restructured the presentation of the numerical results to
emphasize interpretation first, followed by supporting statistics. These revisions collectively improve the
clarity, accessibility, and biological framing of the SCARlink analysis.
Results: Colocalization of IBD-associated SNPs with CREs and DE genes
This section is better structured, but could still be made more efficient:
• Lists of SNPs and genes (e.g., PTGER4, SATB1, GPR183) are too long and could be grouped
more compactly.
• The biological meaning and clinical relevance of the PTGER4 findings should be more clearly
emphasized.
• Redundancy about PTGER4 could be trimmed slightly.
Suggestions:
• Highlight the major discoveries first (especially PTGER4), and summarize other loci briefly.
• Link the findings more explicitly to mechanisms of IBD pathogenesis.
R: We thank the reviewer for the helpful feedback. In response:
1. We have streamlined the lists of SNPs and genes throughout this section by consolidating
overlapping observations and presenting the PTGER4 locus and associated variants as a single
coherent paragraph. Other loci such as LNPEP, TNFRSF14, IL2RA, CCL20, and CXCR5 are now
described more succinctly in grouped summaries to maintain readability while preserving key
biological insights, such as predicted enhancer activity, peak-to-gene linkages, and supporting
evidence from eQTL and fine-mapping studies.
2. We agree that the biological and clinical relevance of PTGER4 deserved clearer emphasis. We
have revised the text to make our findings more interpretable and mechanistically meaningful.
Specifically, we now highlight that:
2.1 PTGER4 expression is strongly predicted by chromatin accessibility (Spearman R² =
0.244 from SCARlink analysis);
2.2 Multiple IBD SNPs colocalize with enhancer regions linked to PTGER4 across diverse
T cell subsets;
2.3 These findings converge on the PTGER4 locus as a genetically and epigenetically
regulated target in T cells, strongly implicating PGE2–EP4 signaling in IBD pathogenesis;
2.4 The SNP rs10440635 is located in an IBD credible set, was previously implicated in
ankylosing spondylitis, and regulates PTGER4 in synovial biopsies, adding cross-disease
relevance.
3. To address redundancy, we have removed repetitive mentions of colocalization results and
merged previously separated pieces of evidence (e.g. SCARlink predictions) into integrated
summaries for each key region.
4. Finally, we have added a concluding sentence that explicitly links these colocalization results
to mechanistic insights, emphasizing how genetic variants may influence cell type-specific
regulatory programs that contribute to IBD pathogenesis.
Results: Application to Other Immune-Mediated Diseases
The extension to other diseases is an important point but could be framed more cleanly:
• Again, the lists of SNPs and genes are too long and detailed for the main text.
• A short summary of the main diseases and key findings at the start would help.
• The clinical relevance of connecting CD8+ memory T cells to psoriasis, Behçet’s, and SLE could
be emphasized more clearly.
Suggestions:
• Summarize the major disease associations upfront.
• Group minor findings together rather than listing them separately.
• Mention broader translational relevance.
R: We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestions to improve clarity and structure. In the revised
manuscript, we have substantially reorganized this section to highlight the major findings more clearly.
Specifically:
1. We now open the section with a concise summary of the main disease associations, emphasizing
the prominent enrichment of psoriasis-, Behçet’s-, and SLE-associated SNPs in ATAC peaks of
CD8⁺ memory T cells.
2. To enhance readability, we have grouped secondary associations (e.g., those for alopecia areata,
ankylosing spondylitis) into a more compact paragraph, while retaining all corresponding
Supplementary Figures.
3. We have clarified the clinical relevance of the CD8⁺ memory T cell findings by explicitly linking
the genetic enrichment patterns to known effector functions and disease mechanisms in psoriasis,
Behçet’s, and SLE.
4. Finally, we have revised the concluding paragraph to more directly emphasize the broader
translational value of our atlas in illuminating shared regulatory mechanisms and informing future
therapeutic hypotheses across immune-mediated diseases.
Importantly, we preserved all Supplementary Figures to retain the full detail for interested readers, while
improving the narrative focus in the main text as recommended. We hope these revisions address the
reviewer’s concerns.
Discussion
The Discussion undersells the major scientific contributions of this study:
• The opening is too focused on techniques (DOGMA-seq) rather than biological discoveries.
• The important findings regarding PTGER4, Th17/Treg dynamics, and PGE2 in IBD pathogenesis
are not highlighted as they should be.
• There is too much repetition of the Results without synthesis or proposing new models.
• The potential clinical relevance of the findings is understated.
• The final paragraph is too generic; it should more confidently state what new understanding the
study provides.
Suggestions:
• Start with the major biological discoveries, not the techniques.
• Frame a model linking genetic variants, chromatin accessibility, PGE2 signaling, and T cell state
transitions in IBD.
• Highlight translational implications, including PTGER4 as a potential therapeutic target.
• End with a confident, forward-looking conclusion emphasizing the study's impact.
R: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive feedback. In response, we have substantially
revised the Discussion section to better highlight the key biological discoveries and enhance the narrative
synthesis of our findings. Specifically:
1. We have revised the opening paragraph to center the discussion on the biological context and
motivation, rather than beginning with a technical description of DOGMA-seq.
2. We more prominently feature PTGER4 and its dual role as both a dynamically regulated
transcriptional target and a genetically implicated node in the PGE2 signaling pathway. We
emphasize its potential as a translationally actionable therapeutic target in IBD, aligning with the
reviewer’s request to highlight clinical relevance.
3. In the revised Discussion, we propose a model in which PGE2 modulates T cell fate transitions
in an activation-state-dependent manner, intersecting with inherited susceptibility through
chromatin remodeling and gene regulation. We further describe how PGE2 selectively represses
effector programs in activated cells while priming resting cells, offering a novel perspective on
how IBD-relevant microenvironment and genetic factors interact in shaping T cell responses
during disease pathogenesis.
4. To reduce repetition, we have streamlined descriptive results and refocused on conceptual
insights, including the regulatory convergence between responses to PGE2, chromatin
accessibility, and GWAS SNP enrichment in Th17, Th1, and Treg cells.
5. Finally, we have strengthened the concluding paragraph to more confidently articulate the
mechanistic model proposed by this study. Rather than ending with a generic summary, we now
explicitly state how our multi-omic atlas enables identification of disease-relevant regulatory
mechanisms and offers a path forward for precision immunomodulation in IBD and other immune-
mediated disorders.
We believe these revisions significantly improve the clarity and impact of the Discussion. We are grateful
for the reviewer’s insightful suggestions, which helped us better articulate the biological significance and
translational implications of our findings.
Reviewer #2:
Remarks to the Author:
The authors conducted an elegant multiomic analysis to explore the connection between inflammatory
bowel disease (IBD) and genetic predisposition, applying a sophisticated computational workflow that,
to the best of my knowledge, has not been previously implemented. Their approach is undoubtedly innovative
and contributes valuable insights.
However, the manuscript's structure and flow present challenges, making it difficult for a broad readership
to follow. The extensive use of technical terminology and abbreviations complicates the overall clarity,
potentially obscuring the manuscript's key message.
Despite the novelty of the computational approach and the compelling nature of the study, the work lacks
mechanistic validation of its findings in IBD, which appears to be the primary aim as suggested in the title.
Given the complexity of IBD pathogenesis, attributing T-cell inhibition solely to PGE2 seems overly
simplistic. A broader perspective incorporating additional mechanisms underlying T-cell-mediated
immunity in IBD would enhance the work’s depth.
I strongly recommend that the authors refine and streamline the text to improve accessibility while
emphasizing the relevance of their findings to IBD pathogenesis. Expanding the discussion beyond genetic
associations to highlight key inflammatory and immune-mediated pathways—fundamental aspects of
IBD—would significantly strengthen the manuscript's clinical impact.
R: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. In response to these
valuable suggestions, we have made the following revisions to improve the clarity and impact of our
manuscript:
1. We have revised the Introduction and Discussion sections to better highlight the key biological
questions and major discoveries of the study. Specifically, we have restructured the Discussion to
highlight our central findings: the activation state-specific effects of PGE2, its differential
reprogramming of Th17, Th1, and Treg cells, and the mechanistic insights into PTGER4 regulation.
We have also incorporated a conceptual model describing how PGE2 may intersect with genetic
risk variants and regulatory elements to modulate T cell phenotypes relevant to IBD. In doing so,
we have shifted technical descriptions of the DOGMA-seq assay and computational pipelines to
the Methods section, thereby improving accessibility for a broader readership and reducing the
technical density of the main text.
2. To further enhance clarity, we have moved several technical descriptions related to the activation
score to the Methods section. In addition, we have added a table of abbreviations in the
Supplementary Table 18 to assist readers in following the manuscript.
3. In response to the reviewer’s concern about oversimplification of attributing T cell inhibition
solely to PGE2, our study did not aim to fully recapitulate the complex mucosal microenvironment
of IBD. Rather, we used a reductionist approach to study the effects of PGE2, TGF-β, or PGE2
and TGF-β in T cells that were also exposed to activation stimuli, IL-1β, and IL-23 based on
rationales described in the Introduction and the Discussion. We intentionally studied T cells from
healthy, young adult donors to avoid confounding variables such as effects of IBD-directed
medications, comorbidities, and aging on the immune responses that we aimed to study, and to
align with the typical age of IBD onset in adults. Within this well-controlled experimental system,
the observed inhibition and reprogramming effects were indeed primarily attributable to PGE2.
We now more explicitly communicate the motivation for our experimental design and
acknowledge its limitations in the Discussion. Given the current lack of high-resolution single-cell
multi-omic studies specifically investigating the effects of PGE2 in human T cells that are exposed
to activation stimuli, IL-23 and IL-1β, which play key roles in Th17 biology and IBD pathogenesis,
we believe that our dataset lays important groundwork for future patient-based studies.
4. Finally, we have expanded the Discussion to better establish relevance of our findings within
the broader framework of IBD pathogenesis and immune-mediated inflammatory pathways. In
particular, we emphasize how PGE2 signaling interacts with T cell activation states and genetic
architecture, including loci like PTGER4, to modulate transcriptional and epigenetic programs.
We also highlight the translational relevance of these insights, especially the potential of the EP4
receptor for PGE2, encoded by PTGER4, as both a genetically regulated effector and druggable
target. In addition, we point to the broader utility of our single-cell multi-omic T cell atlas as a
resource for exploring shared effector circuits across multiple immune-mediated disorders. While
we acknowledge that functional validation remains an important next step, our study establishes a
mechanistically grounded framework and a set of actionable hypotheses for future investigations,
ranging from CRISPR perturbation studies to patient-derived T cells and in vivo disease models.
We are grateful for the reviewer’s comments, which have helped us improve the clarity, focus, and clinical
relevance of our manuscript. We hope that the revised version more effectively communicates both the
conceptual novelty and the broader translational potential of our findings.
Reviewer #3:
Remarks to the Author:
As a reviewer coming from a clinical/transational background, I am not in a position to fully evaluate the
technical aspects of the DOGMA-seq single-cell multiomics platform. However, I find the
characterization and depth of analysis regarding the number and subsets of T cells quite impressive and
commendable.
That said, I believe the claim that this constitutes a model of IBD inflammation—based solely on in vitro
stimulation of T cells with IL-1β, IL-23, and either PGE2, TGF-β, or both—appears overly simplistic.
While the approach clearly identifies key response elements to these specif-ic immune mediators, it does
not recapitulate the complex immunopathology of IBD as seen in patients.
In line with this, I would have appreciated data derived from the DOGMA-seq platform on mucosal T
cells obtained from IBD patients, both during remission and active disease, or from other immune-
mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs), to strengthen translational relevance.
Finally, I would encourage the authors to reflect on whether their DOGMA-seq platform data provide any
insights into the potential relationship between PGE2 signaling and non-response to anti-TNF therapy,
an important and clinically relevant area that may benefit from the mechanistic resolution their platform
enables.
R: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and constructive comments, and for recognizing
the depth and quality of our T cell characterization. Below, we provide point-by-point responses.
1. We agree with the reviewer that our in vitro model cannot fully recapitulate the complex
mucosal microenvironment of IBD. As clarified in the revised Introduction and Discussion, our
goal was not to simulate the full immunopathology of IBD, but rather to model key aspects of
IBD-relevant immune signaling, focusing on the effects of PGE2, TGF-β, or PGE2 and TGF-β in
T cells that were also exposed to activation stimuli, IL-1β, and IL-23 based on rationales described
in the Introduction and the Discussion.
Importantly, we intentionally used T cells from healthy, young adult donors for several reasons: a)
To avoid confounding effects from immunomodulatory or biologic therapies often used in IBD
and other immune-mediated diseases, which could influence T cell responses in unpredictable
ways; b) To exclude potential confounding from immune aging, ensuring more consistent T cell
biology across donors; c) The age range of our study subjects aligns with the peak onset age for
IBD in adults, improving the relevance of our findings.
Moreover, because there are currently no published single-cell multi-omic datasets focused on
PGE2-mediated changes in T cells from healthy human donors that are also exposed to activation
stimuli, IL-23 and IL-1β, which play key roles in Th17 biology and IBD pathogenesis, our study
provides a necessary and well-controlled foundation for future work on patient samples. While
patient-derived mucosal T cells would indeed further enhance translational relevance, such work
is beyond the scope of the current study. However, we fully recognize its value and plan to pursue
this in future research.
2. We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestion to consider potential links between PGE2
signaling and non-response to anti-TNF therapy2, a clinically important and timely direction. In
our dataset, we observed that TNF expression was significantly downregulated across nearly all
activated T cell subtypes (with the exception of CD4+ regulatory and Gamma Delta cells) upon
PGE2 stimulation. This may reflect a feedback mechanism by which PGE2 suppresses TNF-
mediated effector responses, aligning with its known anti-inflammatory roles in certain contexts.
Furthermore, recent single-cell RNA-seq studies in IBD patients have shown that non-remission
anti-TNF ulcerative colitis patients exhibit elevated expression of IL21, TNFRSF1B, and immune
checkpoint genes (LAG3, CTLA4, TNFRSF4, TNFRSF18, HAVCR2) in Th17 cells3. Using this
gene set, we computed an anti-TNF non-remission module score and found that PGE2-stimulated
Th17 cells consistently showed significantly higher scores in both resting and activated states
(Figure 1A–B; Wilcoxon rank-sum test: P = 0.00014 for resting, P < 2.2×10⁻¹⁶ for activated).
These findings suggest that PGE2 exposure may be associated with poor anti-TNF responsiveness
in Th17 cells.
Figure 1. PGE2 promotes T cell states associated with anti-TNF non-response in Th17 cells.
(A–B) Anti-TNF non-remission module scores (based on IL21, TNFRSF1B, LAG3, CTLA4,
TNFRSF4, TNFRSF18, and HAVCR2) in resting (A) and activated (B) CD4+ memory Th17 cells
under IL-1β/IL-23 stimulation with or without PGE2. Module scores were significantly elevated
in PGE2-stimulated cells in both states (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, P = 0.00014 for resting, P <
2.2×10⁻¹⁶ for activated), indicating a shift toward T cell phenotypes observed in anti-TNF non-
responders.
(C) Drug2cell analysis showing reduced predicted sensitivity to the anti-TNF agent Adalimumab
(CHEMBL1201580) in PGE2-stimulated Th17 cells. Scores reflect enrichment of drug target gene
expression mapped to ADALIMUMAB.
(D) Distribution of Th17 cells in WNN UMAP space under IL-1β/IL-23 stimulation with (orange)
or without (blue) PGE2. Reduced Adalimumab target scores in (C) correspond to the PGE2-
stimulated cluster in (D), supporting a potential link between PGE2 exposure and anti-TNF
resistance phenotypes.
To further explore this hypothesis, we applied Drug2cell4 to score enrichment of anti-TNF target
genes in PGE2-stimulated vs. unstimulated Th17 cells (Figure 1C–D). Using target gene sets for
ADALIMUMAB derived from the ChEMBL database5, we found that PGE2-stimulated Th17
cells exhibited significantly lower drug–target scores, implying reduced predicted sensitivity to
TNF blockade (P = 3.27×10⁻¹⁵, FDR = 2.82×10⁻¹⁴, log₂FC = –1.19). Notably, prior studies have
implicated COX-2–PGE2 signaling in impaired epithelial regeneration and reduced
responsiveness to TNF inhibitors in UC6, consistent with our observations. These findings
reinforce the concept that PGE2 may contribute to treatment resistance in IBD by reprogramming
T cells toward non-responder states. While PGE2 can exert anti-inflammatory effects, its
activation of regulatory pathways in Th17 cells, already implicated in anti-TNF non-response—
raises important considerations for therapeutic strategies.
Given the scope and mechanistic focus of the current study, which centers on mapping PGE2-
mediated chromatin and transcriptional changes, we have opted not to include these findings in
the main text. However, we believe they offer a valuable translational perspective and plan to
explore them further in future patient-focused studies that directly integrate clinical treatment
outcomes.
